events.text: For a hundred years the left ridge of your valley has been nobody's: crows, a fox, a pine forest going about its business. One spring night the whole of it moves. In the morning the pines on it stand in a different order, and the mist that comes off them is blue-green and smells of rain. You go down to the saddle between the ridges, lie in the azaleas, and wait. When the long head comes down out of the trees you have your sentence ready, as you have had it ready for a century. "Left ridge," you say. "So. You are what was coming."

choices.text: Wait, and see what it does with its head

effects.log: It does something: a bow, a stare, a question. With dragons it hardly matters which, the first time. What matters is that it does not put one claw on the saddle. You note that down, the way you note everything.

choices.text: Tell it the terms before it can speak: the west side is yours, and has been since before the first house

effects.log: You tell it about the deer, the boar, the old shrine, and you do not tell it about the deep spring that nobody has found yet. A landlord keeps one room locked. The dragon listens to the whole speech, which is more than the last one did.

choices.text: Yawn, enormously, and walk back up your own ridge

effects.log: Let it wonder. A tiger that explains itself is a tiger that can be argued with. From the top of the right ridge you watch it watching the place where you were, for most of the morning.

events.text: A great stag dies in the stream at the bottom of the valley, exactly in the middle: antlers on the dragon's bank, haunches on yours. You come down at dusk to eat it, because dead meat on your bank is your meat, and find the dragon lying in the shallows, considering it.

choices.text: Eat from your side, watching it over the carcass

effects.log: You eat. It does not. When you are done you lick your paws and say, "The stream is the line, then?" It agrees that the stream is the line. The first treaty of the valley, and no human will ever know it was signed.

choices.text: Tear the stag in half, neatly, and push its half across the water

effects.log: It does not eat stag. It eats it anyway, slowly, with the face of someone being polite at a funeral. Some treaties need a meal. You like it a little more for the face.

choices.text: Drag the whole stag up your bank while it watches

ok.log: The stream comes out of its banks behind you as the carcass goes up the slope. The dragon does not stop you. It looks at the empty water with an air of noting something down for later.

fail.log: The stag catches on a root, you heave, and the antlers come away in your jaws and the rest slides back into the stream, onto the dragon's side. Nobody says anything. That is worse. (-10 health)

events.text: The first spring after a hard winter, the clouds come in off the sea, and for the first time in your life they do not come to you. They pile up over the left ridge. Your slope is still brown, the spring under your rock still frozen, your deer thin as ladders. You have never asked anyone for anything. You sit on the right ridge and watch the clouds go to the dragon.

choices.text: Say nothing. What it does with the rain is its own answer

effects.log: A tiger does not ask. Whatever falls on your slope this year, early or late or not at all, you will remember exactly where it fell, and so will the dragon, because you will be watching it remember.

choices.text: Go down to the saddle and say one word across it: "Half"

effects.log: One word, the first thing you have asked of anyone in three hundred years. It costs more than a fight would have. The dragon looks at you a long time, the way you look at a stag that has spoken.

choices.text: Hunt the dragon's side of the valley all spring, deer for deer

effects.log: If the rain is its, the deer that drink the rain are yours. You take four from the left ridge before the azaleas fade. Nobody says a word about it, all year, so loudly that the whole valley feels it.

events.text: People have come into the valley. Eleven households of burnt-out farmers from the south have built mud walls on the flat land between the ridges and called the place Yonggok, Dragon's Elbow, which you think is a little unfair. They put their offerings on a flat rock on the dragon's side. On your side they put nothing. Then a small child from Dragon's Elbow wades the stream after chestnuts and does not come back by dark.

choices.text: Carry the child back across the stream at dusk, by the jacket, very gently

effects.log: You set the child down on the doorstep of the end house and are gone before the door opens. The next morning there is a rice cake on a flat rock on your side of the stream. It is a terrible rice cake. You eat it.

choices.text: Sit on your rock at dusk where the whole village can see you, and let them learn whose side this is

effects.log: The child is home by nightfall, walked to the stream by a tiger and pushed over it with a nose. The village puts a second rock on your side of the stream after that, and a pig's head on it every New Year, and its children are taught to count the stripes from a long way off.

choices.text: Leave the child to the dragon. Its people, its trouble

effects.log: Something long comes down the left ridge in the dark and the child is home before the moon is up. You watch it do it. It does it well. You will not say so.

events.text: A long winter night on the saddle, snow on both your backs. You talk, for once. You tell the dragon about the others: the Black Tortoise with the snake round it in the north, the Vermilion Bird over the southern sea, and the Yellow Dragon of the centre, who once looked at you across a whole province and said nothing at all. "They will ask me about you, one day," you say. "Tell me why you guard. So I know what to say." It answers. You listen. Then it asks you the same.

choices.text: "Because I am the thing people need guarding from"

effects.log: The dragon does not laugh. It turns that over for a long time in the snow. "That is not a reason," it says at last. "That is a confession." You put your head down on your paws and do not talk any more that night, but you are not angry.

choices.text: Tell it about the cave, the mugwort, and the twentieth day

effects.log: You have never told anyone. Your ancestor, the bear, the dark, the hunger that walked out on the twentieth day. The dragon listens to the end. "And you would stay," it says, "if you could." It is not a question, and you do not answer it.

choices.text: "I do not know yet"

effects.log: The dragon makes a sound like a river under ice, which you realise after a while is laughing. "Good," it says. You are not sure what was good. You watch the snow pile on its back until dawn, and feel, for the first time, that you are not the only one keeping this valley.

events.text: A summer storm comes off the left ridge too proud and too fast, and the lightning in it finds the old pine on your ridge where the mountain god's shrine stands. The shrine burns: the plank painting of the old man and his tiger, the offering rock, the straw rope. The storm drifts on, satisfied with itself. The dragon has not even noticed.

choices.text: Go over the saddle and roar it awake

effects.log: You put your whole chest into it from the middle of the saddle. Every bird on both ridges goes up at once. The dragon comes out of its cloud looking, for the first time since it arrived, young. It spends the autumn helping the villagers rebuild. It does not apologise. Neither would you.

choices.text: Challenge it to settle it on the saddle at moonset

ok.log: All night on the saddle, teeth and coils and the azaleas ruined. Neither wins. At dawn you lie three paces apart, bleeding, both pleased. A fight between equals is a kind of greeting the gentle never learn.

fail.log: It wraps you once round the middle and sets you down on your own ridge, not roughly. You learn how big it is. It learns that you will try. (-16 health)

choices.text: Rebuild the shrine yourself, carrying stones in your mouth, where it can see

effects.log: A tiger carrying stones up a ridge one at a time for a month is the strangest thing the valley has ever seen. On the twentieth day a new straw rope is already round the pine when you come up in the morning, tied with a knot no human hand makes. (-6 health)

events.text: Six springs have failed on the right ridge, one after another. The spring under your rock is a damp patch. The paddies on your side of the valley are dust; on the left side they are green to the edges, and the farmers of Dragon's Elbow have stopped saying the right-hand fields are unlucky and started saying they are cursed. In high summer you go over the saddle, thin, your coat dull, and say it: "You take all the rain. You do not even know you are doing it. That is worse."

choices.text: Walk it along your dead springs, one by one, and make it put its nose in each

effects.log: Nine dead springs. Whatever it understands at the ninth, it understands slowly. You do not help it. A grievance that is explained is only a complaint.

choices.text: Say it, and go back over the saddle, and give it nothing more

effects.log: You do not wait for the answer. Let it sit with the sentence on its own side of the stream for a year. You have sat with the clouds for six.

choices.text: Ask nothing of it. Take the grievance to the mountain god instead

effects.log: The old man of the mountain listens with his eyes shut and says, "Count the streams." That is all. It is, you will find, a great deal.

events.text: You bring witnesses: a mountain spirit from the next range, the old badger who has counted streams on this saddle for nine hundred years, and your grandmother, the ancient tigress of the far saddle, who is enormous and toothless now and sits on the saddle like a snowdrift. They count the streams between the ridges, stone by stone, for nine days. On the tenth the count is clear: seven streams run left, two run right.

choices.text: Accept whatever it offers, and ask only that it watches the count every spring

effects.log: Whatever it gives up, it gives up. Your grandmother watches the whole thing without a word and then nods, once, at you, not at the dragon. It is the first time she has done that since you were a cub.

choices.text: Demand the roots under the saddle pulled out, now, all of them

effects.log: "Now," you say, and your grandmother sighs through her gums like wind in a cave. Justice asked for too loudly sounds the same as greed. The badger writes something down.

choices.text: Let your grandmother speak for the west

effects.log: She says very little. When the dragon offers rain every third year, she says, "A gift is a leash," and goes back to sleep. You think about that for a hundred years, and so, you suspect, does the dragon.

events.text: A drought year for everyone, left and right. Heaven has sent nothing. Both valleys are cracking, and there is one deep spring left on the saddle between the ridges, the one you never told anyone about, enough for one side. You are lying beside it already when the dragon comes down.

choices.text: Lie on your side of it, and share it, cup by cup

effects.log: A summer of a tiger and a dragon on either side of one spring, dividing the water with a gourd ladle the villagers left. Both valleys are thin by autumn. Neither is dead. Once you wake with your head on its claw and decide you did not.

choices.text: Fight for the spring. The right side has been dry for six years

ok.log: You win. The right side drinks. On the left they bury their old people that winter, and the dragon looks at you from its ridge with an expression you will meet again at the council of four.

fail.log: You lose. It does not even hurt you more than it must. It drinks, lets the water run left, and goes back up its ridge. (-25 health)

choices.text: Get up and give it the spring. Feed your side another way

effects.log: All that winter you leave deer at the doors of the right-hand farms at night, one house at a time, and never the same house twice. The dragon watches you do it from the saddle and says nothing at all, which from a dragon is a hymn. (-8 health)

events.text: In the dry years a farmer from your side of the valley went over the stream at night with a bucket and a hoe and cut the dragon's farmers' ditch. Dragon's Elbow caught the farmer at dawn and dragged the farmer to your shrine at the autumn equinox, because a quarrel over water and ditches belongs to Legs, the first mansion of the West, and every child in the valley knows who sits in that court.

choices.text: Look at the farmer's hands, the bucket, and the child coughing at the back of the crowd

ok.log: One bucket, cut from the ditch, carried to a child with the summer fever. You pardon the farmer, and order the ditch mended by the farmer's own hands before the frost, on the left side, every stone. The magpie files it under Legs. It was just.

fail.log: You pardon, because the farmer weeps. Later you learn the ditch was cut three times, not once, and the water went to a landlord's paddy. Not every tear is a fact.

choices.text: Punish: the farmer goes over the stream and serves the left side a year

effects.log: A year of carrying water for the people whose water was stolen. Fair, perhaps, if you did not know about the child. You did not ask. The magpie does not file it.

choices.text: Send for the dragon to sit beside you. It is its ditch

effects.log: The two of you hear the case from either side of the stream, and the farmers of Dragon's Elbow never forget the sight. One bucket, a sick child, a ditch to mend. Two judges agree. The magpie files it under Legs, and adds a note in the margin about the dragon's manners.

events.text: Many years after the drought you go over the saddle in the first snow and sit down at the head of the left ridge. You are old now, even for a tiger that does not die: grey at the muzzle, slow on the scree. "The grievance," you say. "I have come to close it, or keep it. Your choice, for once."

choices.text: Close your eyes and wait for its answer

effects.log: It answers. Whichever word it chose, it chose it, and for once the choice was not yours. That was the gift. The snow goes on falling on both of you until morning.

choices.text: Tell it what it still owes you, at length, with examples, before it can answer

effects.log: It takes most of a winter night. At the end of it you put your forehead against its brow, the way tigers do with their own kind, and whatever it says next, you have already forgiven it.

choices.text: Laugh, and say: count the streams with me every spring, for ever

effects.log: A grievance kept is a grievance tended. Every spring after this one, a tiger and a dragon walk the saddle counting water, arguing about the fourth stream, which has never been anybody's.

events.text: You have a cub. The other parent, a tiger of the next mountain, left it at the boundary oak with a look that said your turn. It is white, barred with black, the size of a dog and twice as foolish. It falls into the stream every day. It has tried to eat a hedgehog four times. It thinks the magpie is its friend.

choices.text: Teach it to stalk, belly in the snow, the way you were taught

effects.log: It learns everything except silence. By autumn it can stalk a deer to within a stone's throw and then sneeze. You are prouder than you will ever admit.

choices.text: Let it fall in the stream until it learns not to

effects.log: It does not learn not to. It learns to swim. This is not the lesson you meant, and it is a better one.

choices.text: Teach it to fish with its tail through the ice, as the old rabbit story says

effects.log: You let it learn the hard way, as the story says: the ice closes, and it leaves a tuft of white tail behind, and howls. Then you break the ice and lick its tail and tell it about the rabbit. It is the first story you have ever told anyone.

events.text: The magpie brings word from the west: the mountain god wants you for a season beyond the far ranges, and a season is too long for a cub that falls into streams. One spring morning you pick it up by the scruff and stand at the edge of your ridge, considering your options. None of them is good.

choices.text: Drop it on the saddle in front of the dragon: "Watch it. If it dies, we are enemies. If it is spoiled, also"

effects.log: The dragon looks at the cub. The cub looks at the dragon, then climbs its nose. You walk west without looking back, because if you look back you will not go.

choices.text: Leave it with your grandmother, the ancient tigress of the far saddle

effects.log: Your grandmother opens one eye, sees the cub, and closes it again. The cub burrows into her side like a flea into a snowdrift. You go west with the feeling that you have handed something small to something very old, which is what grandmothers are for.

choices.text: Take it west with you, in your mouth when it tires

effects.log: Three hundred miles with a cub in your jaws for half of them. It sees the western ranges, the salt flats, a black bear, the mountain god of another country. It will never stop talking about it. (-10 health)

events.text: You come back over the saddle at the end of the season. The cub is alive, wet, smug, and smells of pine and river. It will not say what the dragon did all season, and the dragon will not say either. They exchange a look you do not like at all.

choices.text: Say: "Spoiled. But alive"

effects.log: The dragon takes it as the compliment it is. The cub takes it as permission, and you spend the next ten years fishing it out of things.

choices.text: Count its legs. Nod. "Correctly done"

effects.log: Four legs, two ears, one tail with a white tip like yours. It is the most you have ever said to the dragon. It seems to know that.

choices.text: Say nothing, and owe it

effects.log: A tiger in debt. You carry it like a thorn in a pad, and you do not pull it out, because you might need to remember it.

events.text: Your grandmother gives the cub back at the end of the season with one sentence, which the cub repeats to you with enormous gravity the whole way home: "A tiger who never forgives is a trap. A tiger who always forgives is a rug." It does not know what a rug is. It has decided it does not want to be one.

choices.text: Ask it which it would rather be, then

effects.log: "A trap," it says at once, then thinks for a whole afternoon and says, "No. Neither." Your grandmother taught it in a season what took you three hundred years. You are not jealous. You are a little jealous.

choices.text: Tell it that the old one taught you the same, and you are still learning it

effects.log: It finds this very funny. A tiger as old as a mountain, still learning. It tells the magpie, who tells everyone.

events.text: The cub came home from the west different: quieter, with a long scar over one eye from the black bear and a way of looking at the horizon that you recognise from the reflection in the stream. Tonight it asks you why the mountain god of the west had no tiger.

choices.text: "Because his tiger went into the human world and stayed"

effects.log: It is the truth, or the truth as the magpie told it. The cub thinks about that for a long time, and you watch it think, and wonder which of you the story was for.

choices.text: "Because his tiger ate one traveller too many"

effects.log: Also true, by another magpie. The cub goes very still, and that night it sleeps against your side for the first time since it was blind.

events.text: The cub is grown: a white tiger of its own, almost as long as you, and still faintly ridiculous around the ears. It sits on the boundary oak where its other parent left it, all those years ago, and asks your leave to go and find a mountain.

choices.text: Drive it off with your teeth, as you were driven

effects.log: It is the only way a tiger has ever been taught to leave. It runs, bleeding a little from one ear, and stops on the far ridge and looks back, and then it goes. You lie under the boundary oak for a week.

choices.text: Walk it to the edge of your land and show it the next mountain

effects.log: You walk side by side to the last scent-tree. There you stop, and it does not. That is all the ceremony tigers have, and it is enough.

choices.text: Give it your old pass, the one you held when you were young

effects.log: Somewhere three valleys over, travellers start crossing an old pass in groups of ten again, and a white-tailed tiger sits on the rock above the bend at dusk, sneezing.

events.text: Your three littermates, who followed the roads to where the people are, hold the eastern hills now. They are bigger than you and older in everything that matters to a hunter. In the last ten years the villages under them have buried fifty. The magpie comes to your rock at dusk with its feathers on end. Heaven has spoken: one of the three must die, on a human blade, at the spring pagoda-circling.

choices.text: Go to them tonight and warn them

effects.log: You run the whole night through the eastern hills, and on the way you pass three straw sandals in the snow, all left feet, each from a different traveller. You are not sure, by the time you get there, what you mean to say.

choices.text: Heaven is just. Fifty is fifty

effects.log: You say it aloud to the magpie, so that someone hears it. The magpie looks at you sideways, the way it looks at a worm it has not decided about.

choices.text: Go to the mountain god and ask whose blade

effects.log: The old man of the mountain will not tell you the name. He tells you only that it is someone who has circled a pagoda all night before, and that you know the one.

events.text: The den in the eastern hills stinks of old blood and lamp oil from a peddler's pack. Your three brothers lie in it like boulders. The eldest, the one with the spear scar across the nose, listens to you and laughs. "We are what you would be," it says, "if you were honest about your teeth."

choices.text: Fight the eldest until they promise: no humans for ten years

ok.log: It is a long fight in a small den. When it is over the eldest licks its torn ear and promises, and the other two promise because the eldest did. Ten years. Heaven is not counting in tens.

fail.log: The eldest was always bigger. It pins you by the throat in the lamp-oil dark and lets you go, contemptuously, as a gift between kin. (-22 health)

choices.text: Hunt with them one night, to remember what you came from

effects.log: You take a red deer. They take a ferryman. You stand on the bank in the moonlight and watch them eat, and you do not stop them, and you do not join them, and you are not sure which is worse.

choices.text: Tell them about the cave, the bear and the twentieth day

effects.log: The middle brother listens. The other two sleep. At the end the middle brother says, quietly, "Our ancestor was hungry. So are we. That is the whole story." It is not the whole story. It is the part they have chosen.

events.text: The spring lantern festival at the temple below the eastern hills. In a human shape, pale-haired and barefoot, you join the crowd circling the stone pagoda with their wishes. All night one young hwarang keeps circling beside you, a sword wrapped in silk on the back, feathers in the hat, saying nothing. Toward dawn {npc} finally speaks. "I have been sent to kill a tiger," {npc} says. "I have never killed anything. Is it wrong to pray first?"

choices.text: Keep circling with {him} until the lanterns burn out, and speak of anything but tigers

effects.log: You talk about the moon, the temple carp, a song from Gyeongju neither of you can sing. By dawn {npc} has forgotten to be afraid. You have not. You know what heaven sent {him} for.

choices.text: "Pray. Then come to the pagoda grounds in three nights, and look carefully at what comes"

effects.log: {npc} stops walking. "How do you know when it will come?" You do not answer. You go round the pagoda one more time and are not there when {npc} looks again.

choices.text: Leave the circle before {npc} can say any more

effects.log: You walk out of the lanterns and up into the dark of the hills, and do not look back, which is how you know you wanted to.

events.text: Three nights later. {npc} waits at the pagoda with the sword unwrapped and a single lantern. Thunder walks along the eastern hills with nothing under it. Your three brothers are coming down to the temple, because heaven has told them where, too. You stand in the dark at the edge of the lantern light in your own shape, white-tailed, and {npc} sees you.

choices.text: Step into the light and say: "It was me at the pagoda. Look at me"

mem.note: circled the pagoda with me, and were a tiger

effects.log: {npc} looks. The sword-point drops an inch, then lifts again, and stays lifted, and shakes. "I know," {npc} says. "I knew at dawn. I came anyway."

choices.text: Stay in the dark and keep the guise a secret

effects.log: {npc} looks straight at you and sees only a white tiger, one of four, and raises the sword. It is better this way, you tell yourself. You are a poor liar even to yourself.

events.text: Your three brothers come out of the pine dark into the lantern light, one, two, three, and stop. Heaven wants one. The hwarang wants none and has a sword. You are between all four of them, and the thunder is directly overhead.

choices.text: Offer yourself on the blade in your brothers' place, and make {npc} take it

effects.log: You walk onto the sword before {npc} can turn it aside. Heaven is satisfied with a tiger, and does not much mind which. {npc} rises high at court for killing the white tiger of the eastern hills, and spends the honour on a temple by the stream where you fell: Howonsa, the temple the tiger wished for. Every spring, someone circles its pagoda all night alone.

choices.text: Let heaven take the eldest. It has eaten the most

effects.log: You do not move. The eldest goes for the lantern, and the sword meets it, more by terror than by skill. The thunder stops. Your two other brothers go back into the dark without you. {npc} kneels by the dead tiger for a long time, and then by you.

choices.text: Hide all three in the shadow of your stripes and run them north across the river

ok.log: A long night of pine shadows and river ice. At dawn your brothers are across the northern river, in somebody else's mountains, and heaven's thunder is grumbling over an empty temple yard. Heaven does not forget. Neither will the villages up north.

fail.log: The lightning finds the youngest at the river. It was always the slowest. You carry it the last mile anyway, and bury it in the snow on the far bank, and come home with burnt whiskers. (-25 health)

events.text: Twenty years after the night at the pagoda, a small temple stands by the stream where your brother fell. {npc} built it with the court's reward, and named it for a tiger, and does not explain the name to anyone. You come down in human shape on the night of the lantern festival and find {npc} circling the pagoda, greyer, alone.

choices.text: Fall in beside {him}, and circle until dawn

mem.note: came back to circle the pagoda

effects.log: Neither of you says a word all night. At dawn {npc} puts a hand on your sleeve, very lightly, the way one touches a sleeping animal, and goes in to the morning chant.

choices.text: Leave a deer at the temple gate and go

effects.log: The monks find it at dawn and do not know what to do with it, being monks. {npc} knows. {He} buries it behind the hall, with a little bow, as if it were a letter.

events.text: News comes down from the north the way bad news does, on a magpie with a torn tail. Across the river your brothers have found villages that never had a tiger, and they have taught those villages what a tiger is. The people there are building pit traps on every path and burning the forests back from their walls.

choices.text: Go north and bring them back under your eye

effects.log: It takes a winter. Two come back. The third stays, and the northern villages will tell its story for three hundred years as the tiger that ate a whole valley. You did not save them. You only moved them. (-12 health)

choices.text: Lay the dead you made by saving them on your own account

effects.log: They are not your ghosts. You visit every cairn in the northern villages anyway, in the snow, and lie by each one for a night. A shaman up there sees you at it, and that is how the north learns that tigers mourn. (-8 health)

choices.text: Their teeth are their own. You hid them once; that is all you owed

effects.log: You say it to the magpie, and then again to yourself, and it is no truer the second time.

events.text: At the autumn equinox the court sits under the old pine, as it has for two hundred years: you on the flat rock, the magpie on the branch above with a strip of bamboo, the mountain spirits at the edge of the firelight. This year the case belongs to Bond, the mansion of crowds. In the spring famine forty people from the river villages broke the doors of the county granary. The granary-keeper says it was a riot. The crowd says it was a loan. Both have come up the mountain in a dream, and both are shaking.

choices.text: Pardon the crowd: hunger is not a crime

effects.log: Forty people go back down the mountain in their dreams weeping with relief. Later you learn three of them carried away silk as well as seed rice. The magpie does not file it. Mercy that does not look is only a softer kind of not looking.

choices.text: Punish the ringleaders: doors were broken, and doors are the law

effects.log: Three ringleaders wake with the marks of your teeth on their doorframes and leave the county by noon. The granary-keeper smiles. The magpie, on the branch, does not write anything down, and you notice.

choices.text: Look closer: who opened the first door, and what did they take?

ok.log: The first door was opened by the keeper's own man, at the keeper's word, so the relief rice already sold upriver could be blamed on a riot. The crowd took seed rice, counted it, and left a tally stick. You pardon the crowd and send the keeper's man running over three ridges. The magpie writes on its bamboo: Bond. It was just.

fail.log: The faces blur in the firelight. You pardon half and frighten the other half, and nobody, including you, is sure why. The magpie files nothing.

events.text: Stomach, Heaven's Granary. The county magistrate has kept the relief granary sealed through two lean winters. Brought up the mountain in a dream, still in a silk nightrobe, the magistrate is calm. "A great famine is coming. I have read the signs. I am saving the rice for it. Would the Lord of the Mountain rather the children eat it now and starve later?"

choices.text: Pardon: foresight is a virtue in a magistrate

effects.log: The magistrate bows and wakes. In the spring you find the granary half empty and the seals unbroken, and a new tile roof on the magistrate's country house. The magpie does not file it.

choices.text: Follow the rice carts by night before you judge

ok.log: Every fifth night a cart leaves by the back gate for the river, where boats take the rice upriver to sell at famine prices. You stand in the road in front of the next cart. The driver runs; the magistrate, when the news reaches the hall, does not sleep again in that county. The seals come off by order of a governor who had a very bad dream. Stomach. It was just.

fail.log: You watch the wrong gate for a month. By the time you judge, the magistrate has been transferred with honours to a richer county. (-6 health)

choices.text: Punish at once: a sealed granary in a famine is a crime whatever the reason

effects.log: You walk into the magistrate's dream with your mouth open and stay there until the keys are handed over. Severity without proof, this time, happened to land on the guilty. The magpie files it under Stomach, with a small question mark.

events.text: Hairy Head, the Pleiades: the star of the northern horsemen and of the gathering in white. A horseman from beyond the northern river has been caught on your mountain with a bundle of bones, and the villages want a raider's death for a raider. Kneeling under the pine, the horseman says only that these are a brother's bones, and that the family buried its dead on this mountain, under a cairn with a deer carved on it, before the border moved.

choices.text: Find the cairn with the deer before you judge

ok.log: It is there, under the moss on the north shoulder, older than the village: a deer, carved by someone who had seen a lot of deer. You let the horseman bury the bones in the old way, in white, and you sit at the edge of the funeral like a guest. Hairy Head. It was just.

fail.log: You do not find the cairn. You pardon anyway, on the strength of a face, and the horseman goes north. You will never know.

choices.text: A raider is a raider. Drive the horseman back over the river

effects.log: The bones go into the river. A year later you find the deer cairn by accident, hunting, and lie beside it for a long time.

choices.text: Pardon: whoever buries a brother has done nothing worth a death

effects.log: You let the horseman bury the bones on the mountain, and the cairn with the deer turns out to be exactly where the horseman said. Mercy, this time, did not have to look. The magpie files it under Hairy Head.

events.text: Net, the hunting cart: hunters and poachers. Up before the court this autumn comes an old snare-setter from the village under the shrine grove, a grey stick of a person who has set wire in the mountain god's grove for thirty years. "For the pot," says the snare-setter. "Only ever for the pot." The village nods. The village eats from that pot, sometimes.

choices.text: Pardon: thirty years of hunger is not poaching

effects.log: The snare-setter goes home. Next spring the grove has no musk deer left at all, and the apothecary in the county town has a new roof. The magpie does not file it.

choices.text: Walk the snare lines yourself before you decide

ok.log: The snares are set for musk deer only, the ones whose glands fetch silver from the apothecary in town, and they are set at fawn height. You tear out every wire and put the snare-setter off the mountain for good, with a long look at the apothecary's gate on the way. Net. It was just.

fail.log: A wire you did not see takes you round the forepaw. By the time it is out, the court has sat without you and the snare-setter has gone home. (-8 health)

choices.text: Punish: the grove is the mountain god's

effects.log: You put the snare-setter off the mountain on principle. It turns out, when the wires come up, that principle and fact agree: musk deer, fawn height, sold for silver. The magpie files it under Net.

events.text: Turtle Beak, the tiger's head: garrisons and armies. A deserter from the northern frontier garrison has been living in a cave on your mountain for a year. The garrison's runners have come for the deserter with a warrant and a rope. The deserter says the captain was selling the garrison's rice and the soldiers were eating bark, and the deserter walked south carrying a comrade who could not walk.

choices.text: Find the comrade

ok.log: A grave at the back of the cave, a small one, dug with a cooking pot, and a soldier's tag on a string. The story was true. The runners go back to the garrison with an empty rope and a story about a white tiger in the road. Turtle Beak. It was just.

fail.log: The cave tells you nothing. You let the runners take the deserter, and then, on the road, you change your mind and scare them off, and nobody, the deserter least of all, can say what the verdict was.

choices.text: Pardon: a starving soldier is not a traitor

effects.log: You sit in the road between the runners and the cave until they go. Later you find the small grave at the back of the cave and the soldier's tag on a string, and the magpie files it under Turtle Beak.

choices.text: A soldier who leaves the wall leaves the wall open. Let the rope take the deserter

effects.log: The runners take the deserter north. The captain selling the rice hangs the deserter on the garrison gate as a lesson to the others. The lesson, it turns out, was not the one you meant.

events.text: Three Stars: the Balance and the Punishment, a life for a life. A young man of the valley killed the moneylender with a fulling club and says it was for his mother: the moneylender took the family's paddy and their ox and laughed. The valley loves him for it. The mother, a small woman with a bent back, has climbed the mountain on her own feet to stand at the edge of the firelight, and has not said a word.

choices.text: Ask the mother what happened

ok.log: It takes her until midnight. The moneylender had forgiven the debt that spring. Her son killed him for the ledger, to burn the other debts and sell them back to the debtors, and used her name because the valley would love it. "I bore him," she says. "Do what you must." You do. Three Stars. It was just, and it was the worst night of the year.

fail.log: She will not speak to a tiger. You pardon the son on the valley's love. Years later the mother dies alone in a hut while her son lives in the moneylender's house, and the magpie looks at you and files nothing.

choices.text: Pardon: a son who strikes for his mother has done what the old books praise

effects.log: The valley cheers. The mother walks back down the mountain alone, in the dark, before the cheering stops. The magpie files nothing.

choices.text: Punish: a life was taken, and the Three Stars weigh lives

effects.log: You give the sentence without asking anyone anything. Only afterwards, at dawn, does the mother tell the magpie what really happened: the forgiven debt, the ledger, her name used like a shield. Severity was right. You were not, quite. The magpie files it under Three Stars and does not look at you.

events.text: The autumn case, as every autumn: two villages, one ditch, and a dry year. Upstream says the water was theirs first. Downstream says upstream moved the sluice stones in the night. Both have brought their headmen and their oldest grandmothers, and the grandmothers have brought their own versions.

choices.text: Hear both sides through the night, and walk the ditch at dawn

ok.log: The sluice stones were moved, and moved back, and moved again, by both villages, for years. You order the stones set in mortar halfway between, and the headmen to share one bowl of makgeolli on the spot. Legs. It was just.

fail.log: The grandmothers outlast you. By dawn you have a headache, a judgement, and no idea whether it was right.

choices.text: Give it to downstream, who have less

effects.log: Downstream cheers. Upstream sulks. Nobody files anything, because nobody knows.

choices.text: Give it to upstream, who were there first

effects.log: Upstream bows. Downstream glares at the mountain all winter. Old rights are a kind of right, and the magpie, unconvinced, files nothing.

events.text: The autumn case: a pit-trap dug on the shrine path has taken a woodcutter's leg. The trap-digger is a boy of fourteen who wanted to catch a tiger and be a hero. The woodcutter's family wants the boy's own leg for it. The boy wants nothing except to stop shaking.

choices.text: Look at the pit, and at who taught the boy to dig it

ok.log: A hunter in the county town sold the boy the stakes and the plan, for a share of the bounty. You set the boy to carry the woodcutter's firewood for three years, and you visit the hunter at night. Net. It was just.

fail.log: You judge the boy and only the boy. Somewhere in the county town, a hunter sells the same plan to another boy.

choices.text: Pardon the boy: a child's foolishness

effects.log: The woodcutter's family curses the mountain all winter. The boy digs no more pits. The magpie files nothing.

choices.text: Punish the boy: a leg is a leg

effects.log: You frighten the boy so badly the boy's hair is white by spring. It does not give the woodcutter back a leg.

events.text: The autumn case: a garrison sergeant marched a press-gang through the valley and took every boy over twelve for the frontier. One mother followed the column for three days and bit the sergeant's hand. The sergeant wants her flogged for striking an officer of the crown.

choices.text: Count the boys, and their ages

ok.log: Four of the boys are eleven, one is nine, and the levy roll says sixteen. You send the young ones home over the ridge at night and the sergeant back to the garrison with a bitten hand and nothing to say. Turtle Beak. It was just.

fail.log: You spare the mother and let the column go. Only later do you learn how young some of those boys were.

choices.text: Spare the mother, and let the levy take its due

effects.log: Half a mercy. The mother goes home without her son and without stripes on her back, and does not thank you.

choices.text: The crown's officer was struck. Let the law have its stripes

effects.log: The law has its stripes. The magpie has nothing to file, and says so, loudly, from every pine in the valley.

events.text: It happens over one winter in the den. You go to sleep striped and white-tailed and wake in the thaw white as the first snow, the stripes faint as ink brushed on wet paper. Five hundred years, near enough. The old books say a tiger's coat turns white at five hundred, and that a white tiger is seen only when the ruler is virtuous. You know nothing about the ruler. You go down to the stream to look.

choices.text: Look for a long time

effects.log: The stream shows you something you do not recognise and know at once: an old tiger and a new one, in one coat. The metal in your breath has a cold edge now, like a blade left out overnight.

choices.text: Roll in the ashes of a charcoal kiln, so the hunters cannot see you a mile off

effects.log: Grey is safer than white. It lasts until the first rain, and then the whole valley sees a white tiger walking out of a grey one, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Stand on the rock above the pass at noon and let them see

effects.log: By evening every village in three valleys knows. By the next new moon, so does the capital.

events.text: The villages have seen the white tiger, and a shaman from the market town has come up to your shrine in the red robe with the bells and the fan, and does not dance. {npc} sits on the offering rock and weeps, bells and all, until the sun goes down. When you come out of the pines {npc} does not run. "So it is true," {npc} says. "You came. Which of the old sayings do you mean? That the king is good, or that the war is coming?"

choices.text: Speak: "Neither. I only grew old"

effects.log: {npc} laughs through the tears, a terrible snort. "Nobody will believe that," {npc} says. "They need it to mean something." You realise, slowly, that from now on everything you do will be made to mean something.

choices.text: Speak: "Tell me about the king, and I will tell you what it means"

effects.log: {npc} tells you a great deal about the king, most of it rumour and some of it the kind of truth only market shamans hear. By dawn you know more about the court than you ever wanted, and you have not promised anything.

choices.text: Say nothing. Lie down beside {him} until the weeping stops

effects.log: A white tiger and a shaman on a rock in the dusk. {npc} stops weeping around moonrise, wipes the face on a red sleeve, and goes down the mountain without asking anything else. In the market town {npc} tells nobody, which is the rarest gift a shaman can give.

events.text: White all through, now, even the eyelashes. Autumn has begun to come when you breathe out: the maples on your ridge turn the week you wake, not the week the frost comes. The magpie says the western sky has noticed you. You lie on the rock and try to feel what it is to be five hundred years old and still hungry.

choices.text: Breathe the metal in, slowly, the way the old ones do

ok.log: You find the cold edge inside your breath and hold it like a blade by the flat. When you let it out, a whole slope of oak leaves lets go at once and comes down like rain.

fail.log: The metal cuts going in. You cough frost for a week. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go and hunt, as if nothing has changed

effects.log: The deer see you a mile off now. You have to learn to hunt all over again, white on green, like a cub. It is the best year you have had in a century.

events.text: The court in the capital has heard of the white tiger, and the court is in trouble: two bad harvests, a comet, and a faction that whispers the king is not virtuous. A white tiger, caught alive and shown in the palace, would settle the question. The governor's hunters come up your road with a cage of oak bars and iron bands instead of spears, a cart, eight oxen, and a great deal of rope.

choices.text: Let them see you, once, and vanish

effects.log: A white flank in the pines, there and gone. The hunters spend a season building a better cage. It is a very good cage. You go and sit in it one night, while they sleep, to see.

choices.text: Break the cage in the night, bar by bar, and leave the pieces in a neat pile

effects.log: In the morning the hunters find the cage stacked like firewood and every rope bitten through at the same length. The captain sends the governor a letter that begins, "Respectfully, no."

choices.text: Walk into the cage, and let them carry you to the capital

effects.log: The hunters do not believe it either. They lock the door with shaking hands and drive the oxen all the way to the capital without sleeping, watching the cage, which watches them.

events.text: The cage stands in the forecourt of the throne hall. Ministers in red robes and black winged hats, generals, eunuchs, a crowd of scholars on the roof of the gate. The king is young, thin, and frightened, and comes down the steps alone, which nobody expected. Behind the king the two factions are already arguing about what you mean.

choices.text: Speak to the king, for the king alone: "I came to see whether it was true"

effects.log: The king hears it. Nobody else does: you made sure. The young face goes very still, and then the king says, just as quietly, "And is it?" "Not yet," you say. The king opens the cage with a royal hand and says to the court, loudly, that the tiger is free because virtue does not cage. It is the first good sentence of the reign.

choices.text: Break out and walk through the capital at noon, down the main road, to the west gate

effects.log: Nobody stops a white tiger walking down the main road of the capital. The markets empty, the gates open themselves. The faction that wanted you as proof of virtue spends a year explaining what the walk out meant. So does the other one.

choices.text: Lie down in the cage and go to sleep

effects.log: A white tiger asleep in the king's forecourt for three days, refusing meat, looking at nobody. On the fourth day the king has the cage carried back to your mountain and opened at the shrine. The court decides that this meant patience. Perhaps it did.

events.text: The cage-hunters, unable to catch you and unable to go home empty-handed, catch an ordinary striped tigress in the next range instead, whitewash her with lime, and load her on the cart. Her two cubs are crying in a den under a rock fall. The cart is at the river ford by dusk.

choices.text: Free the tigress and put the hunters on trial at the ford

effects.log: The lime comes off in the river. The hunters kneel on the gravel and confess, all of them, to a forgery against the throne, a poaching, and a theft of two cubs' mother. You send them home to the governor to confess it again. Net. It was just.

choices.text: Free the tigress, and let the hunters run

effects.log: The tigress goes back to her cubs, lime-streaked, furious. The hunters go home and tell the governor the white tiger is a ghost. The governor, who wanted it to be a ghost, believes them.

choices.text: Laugh, and let the painted tiger go to court

effects.log: It rains on the procession at the palace gate. The court sees a white tiger turn striped in front of the throne hall. The faction against the king has the best year it has ever had. The tigress, at least, is let go in the royal hunting park, where she eats a pheasant belonging to a prince.

events.text: Fifty years on, a different king, and not a good one: a reign of forced labour on palaces and a new tax on salt. This king, too, wants a white tiger seen, to prove the old saying. The governor of your province has been promised a remission of the salt tax for the whole province if the white tiger is seen on the mountain once this year by a royal witness.

choices.text: Refuse to be seen. The saying is not a lie you will tell

effects.log: The royal witness waits on the mountain all year and sees nothing but snow. The salt tax stays. In the province they say the white tiger has left because the king is bad, and that saying, at least, is true.

choices.text: Be seen, once, for the province's salt

effects.log: The witness sees you on the rock at dawn and faints. The salt tax is lifted in your province and nowhere else. Somewhere a court chronicler writes that heaven approves of the king. You will carry that line in your stomach for a century.

choices.text: Go into the king's dream as a white tiger with its back turned

ok.log: The king dreams of a white tiger in the throne hall, facing the west wall, which will not turn round no matter what is offered. The next morning the palace works are halted, and nobody at court can say why.

fail.log: The king dreams of a tiger and wakes furious, and orders the chakhogapsa to your mountain. Dreams cut both ways.

events.text: A general of the western command comes up to your shrine alone, in lamellar armour gone dull from a long march, and kneels. The northern horsemen are over the river again, burning. The army marches tomorrow with the four guardian banners, and on its right wing, the white flag of the west. {npc} has come to ask whether the tiger painted on that flag may be you.

choices.text: Give leave: walk out of the pines and let the whole army see you on the ridge

effects.log: Three thousand soldiers see a white tiger on the ridge above their camp at sunrise. Nobody in the right wing will run, this campaign. {npc} looks up at you for a long moment, then rides down the ranks without a word, which is how generals say thank you.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the army means to do with the prisoners

effects.log: {npc} does not answer at once, which is the right answer. "What the law says," {npc} says at last. "And what you say, if you are with us." You give leave, on those terms.

choices.text: Refuse. A tiger's war is not a kingdom's war

effects.log: {npc} bows and goes down the mountain. The banner flies anyway, with somebody's idea of a tiger on it. You hear afterwards that the right wing broke on the second day. You do not know whether it would have held for you.

events.text: The battle on the plain under the northern river. The horsemen come in white, as they always do when they mean to die: the gathering in white of the Hairy Head star. The left wing holds. The centre holds. The right wing, under your banner, is starting to bend. You are on the hill above it.

choices.text: Come down on the horsemen. The tiger comes down

ok.log: Horses will not face a tiger; nothing on four legs will. The charge breaks against you like water on a rock. The right wing does not bend again. By evening the horsemen are back over the river, and you are lying on the hill licking a long lance wound, and every soldier who passes looks up.

fail.deathCause: the northern horsemen's long lances, on the plain under the river
fail.log: There are more of them than there are of you.

choices.text: Roar from the hill until the horses bolt

effects.log: Half the horses turn at your voice and carry their riders off the field whether they like it or not. It is not a glorious way to win a battle. It is a way.

choices.text: Stay on the hill and watch. Men must hold their own wing

effects.log: The right wing bends, breaks, re-forms on the river bank and holds, at a cost you count afterwards, one by one. They did not need you. That is better, and worse.

events.text: After the battle, the general's justice. Eleven of the army's own men ran from the right wing and were caught at the ford. The law says the sword for deserters in the face of the enemy. {npc} has them kneeling in a row by the river and looks up at the hill where you are lying. One of them is a conscript of fifteen. Turtle Beak, the tiger's head: this is your mansion's kind of case.

choices.text: Come down and sit beside the youngest. Let the rest face the law

effects.log: The boy was conscripted at fourteen against the law and put in the front rank with a bamboo spear. The others were old soldiers who ran with the pay chest. {npc} understands at once and sends the boy home. Turtle Beak. It was just.

choices.text: Spare all eleven

effects.log: You lie down in front of the row. {npc} sheathes the sword and spares them all, and three of the eleven, who ran with the pay chest, desert again the next week. Mercy without looking.

choices.text: Let the general's law stand

effects.log: Eleven, the boy among them. The army is very orderly for the rest of the campaign. You do not come down from the hill for three days.

events.text: Prisoners from the north, sixty of them, sit roped in the stubble of a burned field. Their dead lie in rows. They ask, through a merchant who has a little of their tongue, for leave to bury their dead in the old way: in white, with the horses' bridles, facing north. The Hairy Head star stands over the field at dusk.

choices.text: Stand guard over the funeral yourself

effects.log: Sixty prisoners bury their dead in white under the eye of a white tiger, and no soldier of the western army comes within a bowshot to jeer. It is the strangest funeral either country has ever held. Hairy Head. It was just.

choices.text: Drive them north without their dead

effects.log: They go north with nothing. Twenty years later their sons come south in white, and you know exactly why.

choices.text: Leave it to the general

effects.log: The general allows it, grudgingly, and has the bridles taken first. Half a kindness, which the north will remember as an insult.

events.text: Twenty years later the white banner is raised again, in the west, but not for the king. A usurper, a prince with the western command behind the prince's own name, means to march on the capital, and the heralds tell every village that the White Tiger rides with the prince. Your old general, {npc}, is grey now and loyal, and has come to the shrine on a stick.

choices.text: Go to the usurper's camp and lie down in front of the banner, facing away from the capital

effects.log: Ten thousand men see the white tiger refuse their banner. By morning half of them have gone home. The prince goes on to the capital with the other half and loses. The old banner ends up in a shrine on your mountain, where {npc} hangs it with shaking hands.

choices.text: Tear the banner from its pole in the night

effects.log: A white tiger tears a white banner to rags in the middle of an army camp and walks out again. Nobody follows. The rebellion goes on anyway, under a plain flag, and fails anyway. You are not sure you mattered.

choices.text: It is men's business. Stay on the mountain

effects.log: {npc} goes down the mountain without a word. The rebellion fails without you, after a great deal of burning. Your name is on both sides' banners, and you are on neither.

events.text: Death sentences wait for autumn. That is the law: after the harvest, after the equinox, and never on one of the solar terms, never in rain, never before dawn. The ferryman {npc} has waited all summer in the county jail, condemned for drowning the magistrate's son at the crossing. You were on the ridge that night. You heard two voices on the water and one laugh, and the ferryman was not on the boat. The sentence is for the first dry day after the equinox. Tomorrow is dry.

choices.text: Go into the magistrate's dream tonight and show the crossing as it was

ok.log: The magistrate wakes before dawn shouting for the clerk and postpones the sentence, citing an inauspicious dream. The law allows it. The law allows a great many things before dawn.

fail.log: The dream comes out as a white tiger in the river, which the magistrate takes as an omen to hurry. You have to sit on the execution-ground wall all night instead, in plain sight, until the executioner refuses to go in. That works too, for now.

choices.text: Ask the dragon of the left ridge for one day of rain over the county town

effects.log: You go over the saddle and ask. It does not ask why. At dawn a grey cloud the size of a threshing floor sits over the execution ground and rains on nothing else. No sentence in rain. You have bought a season.

choices.text: Find the real killer on the river tonight

ok.log: The magistrate's son had a friend in the boat that night, the son of the richest house in the county, who has not slept since. You find that one on the riverbank at midnight, staring at the water. You do not do anything yet. Severity can wait one more night; you have learned that much.

fail.log: The river tells you nothing. At dawn the ferryman {npc} is taken to the post, and you are on the wall, and you roar, and the crowd breaks and runs, and the executioner with it. The sentence will be tried again. (-8 health)

events.text: The rich house's son, the one who was in the boat. It was a quarrel over a debt, no, over a girl, no, over nothing at all, a shove and a laugh and black water. Since then the ferryman has been waiting to die for it. Three Stars: a life for a life, and this one is yours to weigh.

choices.text: Carry the rich son to the magistrate's yard in your jaws, unhurt, and set the son down in front of the drum

effects.log: The whole county sees it. The rich son confesses on the spot, at length, to everything, including several things nobody had asked about. The ferryman walks out of the jail at noon. Three Stars. It was just, and the human law did the sentencing, which is as it should be.

choices.text: Punish the rich son yourself, on the riverbank

effects.log: Justice and hunger in one bite. In the morning the ferryman is still in the jail, because nobody knows what happened on the riverbank, and a new ghost walks behind you on the pass, calling for its father.

choices.text: Let the son confess unprompted, if the son will

ok.log: You sit outside the rich house all night where the son can see you from the window. At dawn the son walks to the magistrate's gate alone. Three Stars. It was just, and it was not your teeth that did it.

fail.log: The son does not. The rich house hires guards and a shaman. The ferryman waits another season in the jail, and you are back on the wall.

events.text: The ferryman {npc} climbs to your shrine in the first snow with a jar of makgeolli on the back frame and sets it down on the offering rock. Then sits, and looks up at the pines for a long time. "I am told," {npc} says to the pines, "that a tiger sat on the jail wall for me. I would like to thank the tiger. I would also like to know why."

choices.text: Come out and say: "Because you were not on the boat"

effects.log: {npc} nods as if that explains everything, and perhaps it does. Every autumn after that, the ferry at the crossing carries anyone who is condemned and pardoned for free, and there is a white tiger carved on the mooring post.

choices.text: Stay in the pines and let the makgeolli be thanks enough

effects.log: After the ferryman has gone you pour it out on the roots of the oldest pine, all of it. It smells terrible. You keep the jar.

events.text: Another autumn, another sentence somewhere in your mountains waiting for a dry day. The rule has got into your bones: not on a solar term, not in rain, not before dawn. The men who wrote it meant to give heaven time to change its mind. You wonder whether a tiger's judgement should keep the same hours.

choices.text: Take the rule as your own: no verdict of yours on a solar term, in rain, or before dawn

effects.log: From now on the Autumn Court waits for a clear day. Twice in the next century the waiting turns up a fact that changes everything. Heaven, it seems, does use the time.

choices.text: A tiger is not a magistrate. Judgement comes when it comes

effects.log: Quick verdicts, sharp ones. The villages fear your court more, and come to it less.

events.text: The first month, snow on the capital. You have walked three nights down the spine of the mountains to the hill behind the palace, and at dawn you are looking down over the wall into the king's rear garden: a square pond frozen white, a pavilion on red pillars, pines bent with snow, nobody awake but a eunuch with a broom.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Go over the wall and walk the garden, slowly, from the north gate to the pond

effects.log: The eunuch sees you first, drops the broom, and does not scream, which you respect. By the time the guards come, you are lying by the frozen pond as if you owned it. In a sense you were here first.

choices.text: Circle the outer wall once, so the guards on it see you, and go home

effects.log: A white tiger walking the length of the palace wall at dawn, not hurrying. Every guard on the wall sees it. Every one of them tells it differently by noon.

choices.text: Lie down under the pavilion and sleep

effects.log: They find you at noon, asleep, under the floor of the king's favourite pavilion. Nobody dares wake you. You wake at dusk, yawn at forty spearmen, and go.

events.text: The court argues about you for a month. In the throne hall the king says a tiger came into the city once in the old histories of Goryeo, and that it was read as yin strong and yang weak. The Minister of War agrees that it is truly a strange omen. A censor says the hunters should be sent. An old scholar says it is the White Tiger of the West, and that autumn has come to judge the court. Nobody asks you. You can make the omen mean something.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Go back once more and lie down facing the throne hall, very still, for a whole day

effects.log: The old scholar wins the argument. The king, shaken, opens the prisons for the new year and pardons everyone held without trial. A great many of them were held without trial. Autumn came to judge, and chose mercy.

choices.text: Kill the king's hunting hounds in their kennel, and leave

effects.log: The censor wins. The court decides heaven is angry with someone, and it turns out to be three ministers who were stealing from the treasury. A purge. Some of the purged were guilty. Some were only in the way.

choices.text: Leave a dead deer at the door of the palace granary

effects.log: It takes the court a week to agree on what a deer at a granary means, and in the end they agree it means open the granary. In a hungry spring, they do. The capital eats.

events.text: The court has decided to make sure. Three hundred of the royal tiger-catching soldiers are ordered to clear the mountains behind the capital, peak by peak, with musket-men among them now and drums. They begin on the hill where you lay above the palace and sweep west toward your ridge.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Lead them west, slowly, a day ahead, until they are lost in the high ranges

ok.log: Three hundred men follow a white tail into country none of them has seen, and come home in the snow with frostbite and a story. The king hears it and laughs for the first time that year.

fail.log: A musket ball finds your shoulder in a gully. Muskets are new. You learn about them the way tigers learn everything, by bleeding. (-18 health)

choices.text: Go to ground in the old den and wait for the drums to pass

effects.log: Three days of drums overhead. You lie in the dark with your nose on your paws and remember being blind and small in this same dark. When the drums are gone, you come out and it is spring.

choices.text: Let the captain see you, alone, at the head of a gully, and then let the captain go

effects.log: The captain stands there with a loaded musket for a long time and does not fire, and you go, and the captain reports to the court that the mountains are empty. Somebody, at least, was paying attention to the omen.

events.text: A court painter who saw you in the snow garden, or says so, has painted you from memory on a silk scroll: a white tiger by a frozen pond, enormous, kindly, a little cross-eyed. The scroll hangs in the king's study. The painter {npc} comes to your mountain to see whether the memory was right.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Sit for {him}, on the rock, for a whole afternoon

effects.log: The second painting is much better, and much more frightening. {npc} prefers the first one and says so. You find you agree.

choices.text: Let {him} see you cross-eyed on purpose, once, so the first painting stands

effects.log: {npc} laughs until it hurts and goes home satisfied. The cross-eyed tiger hangs in the palace for two hundred years, and every child who sees it decides tigers are friendly. Some of them are.

events.text: The king who saw you in the garden is dead. The funeral procession goes out of the capital along the road under your mountain: the bier, the mourners in hemp, the four guardian banners carried in front, and on the right, the white flag of the west with a tiger on it.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Walk beside the procession, on the ridge above, the whole way to the tomb

effects.log: Mourners in hemp look up and see the white banner below and the white tiger above, keeping pace. It is the only omen in the whole reign that everybody agrees about.

choices.text: Stay away. The dead king was no friend of yours

effects.log: The procession passes. You hear the bells all afternoon from the den. A tiger does not mourn kings, you tell yourself, and lie awake.

events.text: On the far side of the capital, on the slope where you were born in the first snow, a prince is building a detached palace. The geomancers chose the site because the earth there is strong, which it is: there is a tiger under it. They have built the inner hall straight over the mouth of your old den.

choices.text: Walk through the building site every night until the carpenters stop coming

effects.log: It takes eleven nights. On the twelfth there is nobody on the scaffolding but an owl. The prince's steward writes to the capital that the site is unlucky, which it is, for palaces.

choices.text: Let them build. The den has been empty for four hundred years

effects.log: You go and lie on the hill above it the night they raise the ridge beam, and listen to them singing the beam-raising song. It is a good song. You will have to decide later whether to mind.

events.text: The new palace is finished, and the tigers have come. Not you: the young ones of the range, who smell a tiger's den under the floor and come to see whose it is. Two grooms have been taken in a year. The king's ministers want to build a temple on the mountain's tail to press the tiger in the earth down, as the old masters once did with a temple on a tiger's tail, and they are going to cut your boundary oaks to build it.

choices.text: Let them build the temple on your tail. It will keep the young ones off

effects.log: The temple goes up with a bell that rings every dawn. The young tigers do not like the bell. Neither do you. That is what it is for.

choices.text: Go into the king's dream: carve tiger stones with a grin, and face them to the mountain

ok.log: Three grinning stone tigers go up at the palace gates, facing your mountain, so like you that you are a little offended. The young tigers see them and go away puzzled. A grin is harder to fight than a bell.

fail.log: The king dreams of a tiger, which the king had been doing anyway. The temple is built, and the hunters come with it.

choices.text: Drive the young tigers off the slope yourself, and let the king move out

effects.log: Four young tigers, one at a time, over a winter. When it is done the palace is safe, and the king moves out anyway, to a palace with a prettier garden. The empty halls over your den fill with swallows. (-12 health)

events.text: A hundred years on, the detached palace is a ruin of pillars and tile, and village children play in the inner hall over your old den. One of them, a girl of eight, has found the den mouth under a fallen beam and is crawling in with a candle.

choices.text: Lie at the mouth and growl, softly, until she backs out

effects.log: She backs out, white as rice, and tells everyone, and is not believed, and grows up to be the village's best storyteller. She tells the tiger in the den every winter for years, and it is always you, and it is always growling softly.

choices.text: Let her look. There is nothing in there but a smell and four hundred years

effects.log: She comes out with a tuft of striped fur, the first fur you ever lost, and keeps it in a silk bag all her life. You do not know why that pleases you so much.

events.text: Whatever walks behind you on the pass has begun to walk ahead. At dusk you hear it from your rock: a voice on the road calling a traveller by a pet name, in the traveller's own mother's voice, from round the bend where the pines are thickest. The traveller stops. The traveller turns toward the pines. The ghost wants a replacement, it says, so that it can go free. It is offering you one.

choices.text: Let it bring the traveller to you

effects.log: It is very easy. That is the worst of it. In the morning the old ghost is not free: changgwi promise, and the pass keeps. A new one walks behind you now as well, calling softly for someone of its own.

choices.text: Roar down the pass until every voice on it goes silent

effects.log: The traveller runs down the pass and never crosses it again. The voices are quiet for a year. You are hoarse for a month. (-8 health)

choices.text: Follow the voice into the pines and listen to what it is really calling

effects.log: Under the mother's voice, faintly, there is another name, one it calls over and over when there is nobody on the road. It is not luring anyone, then. It is looking for someone.

events.text: The ghost you followed was a salt peddler, eaten on this pass in a bad winter a long time ago, when you were younger and hungrier. The name it calls when the road is empty belongs to a child in a village three valleys west. The child is old now: a grandmother, the village says, with bad eyes and a good memory.

choices.text: Lead the ghost home, three valleys west, and leave it at the gate

effects.log: The grandmother opens the gate at dawn and stands there a long time, listening to nothing. Then she says the peddler's name, once, the way you say a name you have not said aloud since you were young. In the morning the ghost is gone home. (-12 health)

choices.text: Not yet. A ghost that is looking for someone does not lure strangers

effects.log: You leave it calling. It is, at least, an honest ghost. It is still yours.

events.text: The ghosts lead now. They walk the pass at dusk in a line, each calling in a different mother's voice, and the villages have stopped crossing even in tens. A peddler's cart lies on its side at the bend with the ox gone. Hunger is no longer something you feel; it is something your ghosts arrange for you.

choices.text: Follow them. They know the road better than you now

effects.log: Another voice joins the line. The pass is theirs as much as yours, and a little more theirs every year. Somewhere above you, very far away, the magpie stops coming to your rock.

choices.text: Take one of them home the hard way: find its family and walk it to the door

effects.log: A charcoal burner's ghost, home to a kiln in the next valley where a grandson burns charcoal still. The rest of the line watches you go and come back, and is quieter for a year. (-14 health)

choices.text: Stand in the middle of the road at dusk and make the line walk round you

ok.log: They come round the bend calling, and find you in the road, and stop. A long night. In the morning they walk behind you again, where ghosts belong.

fail.log: They walk through you. It is like swallowing ice. In the morning they are still ahead. (-15 health)

events.text: A shaman comes up the empty pass alone, a thin person in a white robe with a rice-steamer pot on the back frame, an iron spindle and a bundle of white paper. {npc} sets up at the bend where the cart lies, burns the paper, turns the pot over on a cairn, and begins to call the ghosts by name, one after another, gently, as if calling children in for supper. Then {npc} turns to the pines and says, "And yours? What do they call you?"

choices.text: Come out and give {him} your name

mem.note: told me your name at the cairn

effects.log: {npc} says it back to you, once, and puts it into the call, and two of the voices on the pass go into the pot and do not come out. The spindle goes through the hole in the bottom. "The rest are yours to bring," {npc} says. "I can only open the door."

choices.text: Drive {him} off the pass

effects.log: {npc} goes, without hurrying, leaving the pot on the cairn and the spindle beside it. You find yourself sitting by it all night.

choices.text: Watch, and say nothing, until {he} is finished

effects.log: One voice goes into the pot before dawn, the oldest. {npc} packs up and goes down the pass, and at the bottom turns and bows to the pines, to you, as to someone who has been helped and does not know it.

events.text: The line on the pass has grown long. In a still dusk the voices ask you something they have never asked: to come down, at last, and walk in front of them. A tiger ahead, its ghosts behind, the whole mountain silent. They say it gently, in their mothers' voices. Nobody would ever cross this mountain again.

choices.text: Turn your back on the road, and go up to the mountain god

effects.log: The old man of the mountain does not look surprised. "One at a time," he says. "The way you made them." It will take you a century. You begin that night.

choices.text: Go down and walk in front of them

effects.log: The road is very quiet with you in front. The villages below bar their doors at noon. Somewhere a lord of ghosts is being born, and it has your face.

choices.text: Lie down in the middle of the pass and let them talk until morning

effects.log: You listen to every voice. Every name. By dawn you know who each of them was looking for, which is the first step home. You are very tired.

events.text: In human shape you come down to the inn at the ferry crossing: low eaves, a mud yard, makgeolli jars sunk to the neck in the earth, and an innkeeper, {npc}, who looks at your white hair and bare feet and asks your name. You do not have one that a human could say. "Baek, then," {npc} decides, "for the hair," and ladles you a bowl.

choices.text: Take the name, and a bowl of barley tea

mem.note: gave the white-haired stranger a name

effects.log: Baek. It sits on you oddly, like a collar. You ask for barley tea instead of the bowl, which makes the innkeeper laugh, and sit on the porch until the last ferry, listening to the talk: taxes, a wedding, and a tiger in the mountains that everyone agrees is a menace.

choices.text: Pay for the night with a deer left at the back door

effects.log: In the morning {npc} finds a whole deer at the kitchen door, still warm, and a guest gone without a trace. {npc} looks up at the mountain for a long time and then, being practical, starts butchering.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what people here say about the tiger

effects.log: {npc} tells you everything, with relish. The tiger carries filial children home. The tiger eats peddlers. The tiger is a god. The tiger is a story for bad children. "Me," {npc} says, "I leave a bowl out for it on the equinox. Can't hurt."

events.text: A season becomes a year. You wash bowls at the inn, carry water up from the ferry, and learn the names of every regular. Tonight three tiger hunters of the county have come in out of the rain and are drinking at the low table by the fire, talking about the white tiger of the mountain, what its pelt would fetch, which bones go to which apothecary. {npc} keeps looking at you.

choices.text: Serve them, and listen to every word

effects.log: By the end of the jar you know their route, their dogs' names, and which of them is afraid. You pour the last bowl yourself, very politely. They tip you.

choices.text: Sit down at their table and tell them the tiger is a myth

ok.log: You are very convincing. You have a great deal of material. They go home in the morning muttering about a wasted season.

fail.log: One of them, the afraid one, looks at your eyes in the firelight for too long and goes quiet. You leave before morning.

events.text: The day you forget to go back. You realise it in the evening, scrubbing a pot: you have not thought of the mountain since the new moon. The den is cold. The pass is unwatched. A magpie is sitting on the inn's gatepost staring at you with one eye, and {npc} is staring at the magpie.

choices.text: Go back tonight, without a word

effects.log: You are on the ridge by moonrise, on four feet, cold, enormous. The den smells of nobody. The pass has had three bad months without you, and the old man of the mountain looks at you over the pipe and says nothing, which is worse than anything.

choices.text: Stay another year. The mountain kept itself before you

effects.log: The magpie flies off. You go on scrubbing the pot. That night a traveller is taken on your pass by a tiger that is not you, and the village holds the funeral the next week, and you serve the makgeolli at it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth, here, over the pot

mem.note: Baek told me what Baek was

effects.log: {npc} hears it out, then takes the pot from your hands and finishes scrubbing it. "I know," {npc} says. "The bowl on the equinox was always for you. Go home. Come back sometimes."

events.text: {npc} is old, and dying, in the back room of the inn with the paper door open to the river. The grandchildren who run the place now have sent a boy up the mountain with a bowl of makgeolli and a message: Baek should come.

choices.text: Come down in the guise, white-haired as ever, and sit by the bed

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the inn by the ferry
effects.log: {npc} looks at your face, which has not aged a day since the inn was young, and laughs, and says, "Of course." You hold the hand until the river goes dark. The grandchildren never ask who you were. They leave a bowl out on the equinox.

choices.text: Come down as you are, and lie in the mud yard where {npc} can see you through the door

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the inn by the ferry
effects.log: The grandchildren scatter. {npc} turns on the pillow to look through the open door at a white tiger lying in the yard in the rain, and smiles with the whole face, and goes like that.

events.text: Tiger hunters. Forty of them, royal ones, with spears and horn bows and a banner, sent because a white-tailed tiger is the greatest prize a hunter can carry to the king, and the court pays by size and by who strikes first. They have beaters with gongs and dogs, and they are working up your ridge from both ends. By tomorrow noon they will have you between them.

choices.text: Wait in the bamboo on the crest. The left ridge is watching
