effects.log: At dawn a fog comes over the saddle from the left ridge so thick that nobody on your ridge can see a spear's length for three days. The dogs lose the scent. Two hunters fall into a gully. On the fourth day the captain declares the white tiger a legend and goes home. On the fifth you go over the saddle and lie down beside the dragon, close enough to touch.

choices.text: Go up the cliff where nothing on two legs can follow

ok.log: You go up the cliff. Three dogs and a horse that follow too far do not come down. The hunters stand at the bottom and look at the rock for a long time, doing sums.

fail.log: An arrow takes you in the haunch halfway up. You make the top. You do not make it quickly. (-20 health)

choices.text: Lie flat in the bamboo, in the shadow of your stripes, and let them walk past

ok.log: Forty men and their dogs pass within three spear lengths of you. One dog stops, looks straight at you, and decides it saw nothing. You will remember that dog.

fail.log: A dog finds you. You leave it and two spears behind, and a long red line on your flank. (-14 health)

events.text: The captain of the royal tiger-catchers is still here after the others have gone, camping alone at the foot of your ridge with a spear and a ledger. {npc} has done the sums: so much for size, so much for the first strike, so much more for a white tail. {npc} shouts up the slope, unafraid. "I know you can hear me. My grandmother says a tiger once walked a child over this pass at night. The child was Grandmother. I would rather not kill you. I would rather be paid."

choices.text: Come down and talk terms

effects.log: You bring the captain the man-eater from the next range, whole, a month later, and the captain is paid by size for a bigger tiger than you. You never agree to anything aloud. You do not need to.

choices.text: Let {npc} climb, and climb, and never find you

effects.log: A season on your ridge. {npc} finds your scrapes, your dens, your old kills, and never once you. In the autumn {npc} leaves a rice cake on the shrine rock with a note scratched on bark: next year.

choices.text: Break the spear, and nothing else

effects.log: {npc} wakes to find the spear in three pieces across the doorway of the tent and a pawprint the size of a winnowing basket beside it. {npc} sits looking at them for a long time, then laughs out loud.

events.text: The king himself comes to the mountains for the great hunt of the season, the martial exercise the scholars complain trampled their fields: a thousand soldiers in a ring, drums, the king on a grey horse with a horn bow. The ring is closing on your valley. The scholars are right about the fields.

choices.text: Break the ring where it is thinnest, at night

ok.log: You go through a line of soldiers like water through a sieve. By dawn you are three ridges away, and the king, told of it, says the exercise has proved the army's weakness admirably.

fail.log: The ring was thinnest because the musket-men were waiting behind it. (-18 health)

choices.text: Let the king see you, alone, on a rock above the grey horse, and let the king go

effects.log: The king's horse sees you first and stands like a stone. The king looks up, bow half drawn, and then lowers it. Neither of you moves. Then you go. The great hunt ends that afternoon, early, and the king never hunts in your mountains again.

choices.text: Go to ground in the old den and let the ring close on nothing

effects.log: A thousand soldiers and a king find a valley full of deer, two foxes and a badger, who is outraged. The scholars write that the hunt was a waste. It was, for them.

events.text: A pit-trap of the royal hunters, sharpened stakes under brushwood, has caught something on the shrine path: not you, but a girl from Dragon's Elbow gathering bracken, who has a stake through her calf and has been screaming since dawn. The hunters who dug it are camped an hour away and have not come.

choices.text: Get her out, carry her down, and then go and visit the hunters

effects.log: You leave her at her mother's door and spend the night at the hunters' camp, where you fill in every pit they dug on your mountain with your own paws, in front of them, while they watch from the trees. Net: hunters who dig where children walk. It was just. (-6 health)

choices.text: Get her out and carry her down, and let the hunters be

effects.log: She bleeds on your white shoulder all the way to the village, and holds on to your ear. The village never forgets it. The hunters dig more pits. (-6 health)

events.text: The captain {npc} is old, lame from a bear, and retired to a hut at the foot of your ridge with a goat and a ledger full of tigers. Every evening {npc} sits on a stump and looks up the slope. Tonight {npc} calls up it, voice cracked. "I never got you. I want you to know it was not for lack of trying. Come and let me see you once before I die."

choices.text: Come down and lie at the stump

effects.npcPass: old age, at the foot of the white tiger's ridge
effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time, then reaches out and touches your shoulder, once, the place a spear would have gone. "There," {npc} says. "First strike." It is the last thing {npc} says to anyone. You take that as fair.

choices.text: Show yourself on the rock above, out of spear range, for old time's sake

effects.npcPass: old age, at the foot of the white tiger's ridge
effects.log: {npc} laughs, coughs, and lifts the old spear in salute. In the spring the hut is empty and the ledger is on the shrine rock, open to the last page, which has only one entry: the white tiger, not caught.

events.text: The old man of the mountain calls you by the wrong name. Not a wrong name: the name of the tiger before you, whom he sat under this pine with for six hundred years before you were born. He catches himself, laughs, pats your head, and calls you by it again an hour later. The magpie on the branch looks away.

choices.text: Answer to the old name, gently, as if it were yours

effects.log: He tells you a long story about something the tiger before you did, a flood and a lost ox, and you listen as if you remember it. By the end you almost do.

choices.text: Correct him, carefully

effects.log: He looks at you for a long moment and his eyes clear. "Yes," he says. "Yes. You came later." He does not call you by the old name again, and you find you miss it.

choices.text: Ask the magpie how long this has been happening

effects.log: Ten years, the magpie says. Longer, perhaps. He forgets the names of villages, of streams, of the stars. He never forgets the names of the dead. Mountains, the magpie says, forget from the top down.

events.text: The old man is tired today. He holds out his staff, the knotted pine staff that every shrine painting shows, and asks you to carry it for an afternoon while he sleeps under the pine. You take it in your jaws. At once you can feel the whole mountain: a landslide waiting on the north face, a lost child in the gully, a pine dying of age on the ridge, a hunter's pit on the shrine path. All of it is talking at once.

choices.text: Answer what you can before he wakes

ok.log: You let the landslide go where nobody lives, walk the lost child out of the gully with the staff, and let the pine die, because it is time. When the old man wakes you give the staff back, and he weighs it in his hand and says, "Heavier." He sounds pleased.

fail.log: Too many voices. You bring the child out and lose the landslide, which buries a charcoal kiln, empty, by luck. The old man wakes, takes the staff back and says nothing about it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Hold it, and do nothing, and give it back the moment he wakes

effects.log: It is the hardest afternoon you have spent. You hold the whole mountain's troubles in your mouth and touch none of them. He wakes, takes it back, and deals with every one of them before dark, slowly. You watch how.

choices.text: Keep it one day longer than he asked

effects.log: He does not ask for it. He sits under the pine and watches you carry it all the next day. When you bring it back at dusk he takes it without a word, and for the first time in four hundred years you cannot read his face.

events.text: The plank painting in the shrine has faded to two shapes, an old man and a tiger, and the village has hired a painter from the county town to do it again. {npc} spends a week on it, by lamplight, alone, and when the villagers come up to see, the tiger in the new painting is white.

choices.text: Go and look at it at night, when nobody is there

effects.log: The old man in the painting has the real old man's kind, tired eyes and the tiger has your white tail. You lie in front of it until dawn. When you come out, the old man of the mountain is sitting on the shrine step, smoking, and says, "It is not quite you yet."

choices.text: Let the painter see you, so the next one is right

effects.log: {npc} drops the brush. Then picks it up, and adds three whiskers. "They will not believe the size," {npc} says. "I will make you smaller, so they can bear it."

events.text: Snow under the pine. The old man has been quiet all winter. Tonight, out of nothing, he asks it: "When I put this staff down for good, would you want it? Or would you rather go west, to the wall of the sky, where your kind sits? I need to know which, so I can start forgetting the right things."

choices.text: "Not yet. Ask me again when the leaves fall a hundred times"

effects.log: He laughs, a dry sound like a branch breaking under snow. "A hundred autumns. Good. That is about how long I have." You do not ask what he means.

choices.text: "Yes. I would carry it"

effects.log: He nods, slowly, and puts his hand on your head, the way he did the first time, four hundred years ago. It is lighter than it was. Everything about him is lighter than it was.

choices.text: "Let me go west"

effects.log: He is quiet for a long time. "Then I will have to find another tiger," he says, "or another old man." He does not sound sad. He sounds like someone who has been asked to plan a journey.

events.text: A sea turtle is standing on your mountain path in a little black official's hat, a long way from any sea. Its jaw hangs crooked from a long journey. It has been sent by the Dragon King of the Southern Sea, it announces to the pines, to find a certain Mister Rabbit. It means to call "To-saengwon!" Its crooked jaw makes it "Ho-saengwon!", Mister Tiger. Every pine on the mountain hears it. So do you. You come down.
events.arc: The Turtle Who Wanted a Rabbit

choices.text: Come down the whole slope at a stately walk, the way the song says

effects.log: The tiger comes down. You take your time about it. By the time you reach the path the turtle has pulled its head in so far that only the hat is showing, trembling.

choices.text: Answer politely: "Mister Tiger is here. What does the sea want with him?"

effects.log: The hat considers this. Then a small voice from inside the shell explains about the Dragon King's illness, the physician, and the rabbit's liver, the only cure. You find you are enjoying yourself.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You open your mouth over the shell. The turtle's head shoots out and bites you on the chin, and does not let go. (-5 health)

events.text: The turtle, emboldened by having survived a tiger, explains that it is in fact a general of the Dragon King and that it eats tigers for its breakfast in the Southern Sea, where tigers are a common nuisance. It is still hanging from your chin, or it has just let go of your chin, or it is about to grab your chin; with this turtle, it is always one of the three.
events.arc: The Turtle Who Wanted a Rabbit

choices.text: Run away, for the look of it, and give the turtle a story to take home

effects.log: You flee up the mountain roaring in terror. Somewhere in the Southern Sea, for the next three hundred years, a turtle tells the Dragon King's court how it routed the white tiger of the west. You hope they believe it. It is a better story than the true one.

choices.text: Show it where the rabbit lives, for the pleasure of seeing what happens

effects.log: You point it at the rabbit warren in the oak wood. The turtle bows, a little too low, and toddles off. You lie on the slope and wait to see who outwits whom.

choices.text: Laugh, which you have not done properly in a century

effects.log: A tiger's laugh is a rockslide in a cave. The turtle takes it as a challenge and bites your paw, and you laugh harder, and it is the best afternoon of the decade.

events.text: A rabbit you know, the cheekiest one in the oak wood, sits on your shrine rock eating your offering and laughing itself sick. It went to the Dragon King's palace under the sea on the turtle's back, it says, and when they asked for its liver it told them it had taken the liver out to dry on a rock on the mountain, as rabbits do, and must go back for it. And they let it. Now the turtle is on the beach, weeping.
events.arc: The Turtle Who Wanted a Rabbit

choices.text: Go down to the beach and tell the turtle the truth about rabbits

effects.log: The turtle listens with its jaw hanging. Then it says, with great dignity, that it will tell the Dragon King the rabbit was eaten by a tiger. You agree to be the tiger. Some lies are just good manners between courts.

choices.text: Eat the rabbit. It is sitting on your offering

effects.log: It goes down in one bite, still laughing. A rabbit judged you once, long ago, and was right. This one was only funny. You feel no better.

choices.text: Let the rabbit keep its liver and its story

effects.log: It hops off with your offering rice cake in its mouth. You will hear that story told in every market for six hundred years, and you will be in it, coming down the mountain, never quite the hero.

events.text: There is a new tiger on your mountain, and it is the worst tiger you have ever seen: it stalks upright, it steps on every stick, it hunts only at one farmhouse, and it drags every kill to that farmhouse's gate and leaves it there. When you corner it at the boundary oak it does not fight. It says, in human words, "Please. My mother is sick. I learned it from a book. My spouse burned the book. I cannot turn back."
events.arc: The Man Who Became a Tiger

choices.text: Drive it off. A tiger that hunts for a house will be hunted by the house

effects.log: It goes, weeping, which tigers cannot do and it does. Three nights later there is a deer at the farmhouse gate again. It has only moved its den.

choices.text: Listen to the whole story

effects.log: A son of the farmhouse, the old woman's only one. Meat cured her the first winter, and the book in the chest said how. The spouse found a tiger in the yard at dawn and the book on the floor and burned it, screaming. A year now. It still dreams in words.

choices.text: Follow it home, quietly, to see the house

effects.log: A thatched farmhouse at the edge of the forest, a lamp in the window, an old woman coughing behind a paper door, and a person sitting on the step with an axe across the knees, staring at the dark. Both of them waiting for the same tiger, for different reasons.

events.text: The filial tiger still cannot stalk. It loses half its kills, it takes calves when it should take deer, and the village is talking about a hunter. It comes to your boundary oak and lies down in front of you, head on its paws. "Teach me," it says. "Or send me back. Either. I cannot do this alone."
events.arc: The Man Who Became a Tiger

choices.text: Teach it to be a tiger: belly in the snow, the wind in its face

effects.log: It learns. Slowly, then not slowly. By spring it moves like something born to the mountain, and you notice it has stopped speaking in its sleep.

choices.text: Take it to the old man of the mountain, to ask for a way back

effects.log: The old man looks at it for a long time. "There is a way," he says. "It costs the same as the way in. Somebody has to want it badly enough." He looks at you when he says it, not at the tiger.

choices.text: Hunt for the house yourself, one season, so it can rest

effects.log: A white tiger carries a deer to a farmhouse gate every third night all winter. The old woman gets better. The spouse on the step with the axe sees you once, by moonlight, and does not lift it.

events.text: The old woman in the farmhouse has died, in the night, in her sleep, well fed. The filial tiger lies at the grave with its ribs heaving. Then it gets up and looks at the farmhouse, where the spouse who burned the book still lives, and you can see in its shoulders exactly what it means to do.
events.arc: The Man Who Became a Tiger

choices.text: Stand between the tiger and the house

ok.log: It hits you once and you do not move, and it sits down in the snow and howls like a person. You stay with it until dawn. The spouse inside never knows.

fail.log: It goes round you. It reaches the gate. And then it stops, on its own, and lies down there, and you come and lie beside it, bleeding, and that is how the spouse finds you both at dawn. (-15 health)

choices.text: Let it. The book was its life, and it was burned

effects.log: You do not stop it. In the morning there is one ghost more on your mountain, but it is not yours. It belongs to a tiger who was a son, and it calls the son's human name all winter, and the son answers it.

choices.text: Talk to the spouse first, in human guise, at the gate

effects.log: You tell the spouse what is coming, and why. The spouse goes out into the snow, alone, and kneels at the grave beside the tiger, and says the son's name. The tiger does not move. It does not do anything at all.

events.text: Ten years on. The filial tiger has a decision to make, and it has come to your rock to make it in front of you: stay on the mountain as the tiger it became, or go with the old man of the mountain into the cave under the north face, where the way back is said to start, and costs the same as the way in.
events.arc: The Man Who Became a Tiger

choices.text: Tell it to go back. One of us should

effects.log: It goes into the cave in the autumn. In the spring a thin person with very old eyes walks out of the forest to the farmhouse, and the spouse on the step drops the axe. You watch from the ridge until the door closes, and then you go and sit in the mouth of the cave for a while, smelling mugwort.

choices.text: Tell it to stay. It is a good tiger now

effects.log: It stays. It holds the slope below yours for three hundred years, and carries filial children home at night, and never once eats a human. The best tiger on the mountain was born a man.

events.text: A sickness goes through the deer of the whole range in one summer: they stagger, they foam, they lie down in the streams and do not get up, and nothing that eats them lives. By autumn there is no game from the river to the northern passes. The boar are gone. The bears are thin. Your belly is a fist.

choices.text: Go north into strangers' mountains, where the sickness has not reached

effects.log: Two months and four borders. The tigers of the north do not like you and say so. You come home scarred, half fed, and later than you meant. (-14 health)

choices.text: Take cattle from the villages, one ox at a time

effects.log: An ox is a family's whole year. You know that. You take one from each village, spread fair, and the villages hate you fairly.

choices.text: Fast in the den, and wait for the sickness to burn out

effects.log: You lie in the dark and feel the hunger walk round and round you like a second tiger. Twenty days, you think. Your ancestor managed twenty days. (-18 health)

events.text: The famine is not only yours. The harvest failed below too, and the pass is full of refugees going north to relatives who may not want them: families with everything on their backs, old people in A-frames, children carried. At dusk a woman stops under your rock to rest, alone, with a baby, and falls asleep. Your belly says what it says.

choices.text: Lie on the rock above her all night so the wolves stay away

effects.log: She wakes at dawn to find pawprints round her in the frost the size of winnowing baskets, and nothing missing. She goes on north with a story. You go on hungry with a better one.

choices.text: Carry the old people over the pass, one at a time, all week

effects.log: There is a tiger carrying grandmothers over the pass, the refugees say, and nobody believes it until they are on its back. You are weaker at the end of the week than you have been in a century. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take her

effects.log: You take her. The baby is found by the next family on the road, at dawn, crying, and carried north. Behind you on the pass there is a new voice, calling a baby's name, and it does not stop for years.

events.text: In the worst month of the famine the landlord of the river villages has his granary barred and guarded, and sells rice by the cup at ten times the price to people eating bark. Heaven's Granary, the Stomach mansion, is shining over his roof. The guards on the gate have spears and a fire.

choices.text: Break the gate at midnight and stand in it while the villages take what they need

effects.log: Nobody takes more than a sack. The landlord watches from an upstairs window and does not come down, because there is a white tiger in the gateway, licking a paw. Stomach. It was just.

choices.text: Go into the landlord's dream and show the bark-eaters

ok.log: The landlord opens the granary the next morning, weeping, and nobody in the river villages ever knows why. Stomach. It was just, and it was quiet.

fail.log: The landlord dreams of a tiger and hires more guards. Fear works on the greedy, but not the way you want.

choices.text: It is not your granary

effects.log: Three hundred people from the river villages die that winter. The landlord does not. You never fail to notice his house again.

events.text: The deer come back, slowly, from the north: a hind and a yearling first, then a herd. The famine is over. You stand in the oak wood watching the hind drink at the stream and do not take her, not yet, and think about what you did with your hunger this time, and what it did with you.

choices.text: Count it honestly: everyone you carried, and everyone you did not

ok.log: You count every one. When you are finished you are lighter, and the hind is still drinking, and you let her finish.

fail.log: You lose count somewhere in the worst month. That is honest too.

choices.text: Take the hind. Hunger does not count; it eats

effects.log: She is the best meat of the century. You eat her slowly, at the stream, and feel nothing at all except full.

events.text: The mountain god's errand for this stage comes on the magpie's tail: a son in the village under the left end of your ridge beats the old mother of the house. "Punish," says the old man of the mountain, and nothing else, which is the hard part. You go down at dusk and look over the fence. {npc} is splitting wood in the yard, strong, red-faced, muttering. The old mother is at the kitchen hearth with a bruise along one cheekbone, cooking a meal that will be thrown at the wall.

choices.text: Watch the house for a season before you do anything

effects.log: A season of looking over a fence. {npc} drinks when the rice runs out, and the rice runs out often. The old mother lies to the neighbours about the bruises. Once, at night, {npc} sits on the step and weeps, and in the morning beats the old mother for seeing it. You understand the house. You do not forgive it.

choices.text: Go in now and take {him} off the mountain for ever

effects.log: The old man of the mountain said punish. The old man did not say eat. That night a new ghost walks behind you on the pass, and the old mother, alone now in the cold house, weeps for the son who did the beating, because that is what mothers do. The errand is not done.

choices.text: Come to the yard in human guise and speak to {him} plainly

ok.log: {npc} listens to a white-haired stranger say the mountain is watching, sneers, and does not lift a stick for a month. Then the rice runs out again. A warning is a door, not a wall. You have given {him} the door.

fail.log: {npc} throws a log at the white-haired stranger and laughs. That night the old mother pays for the stranger's visit.

events.text: Tonight {npc} has the stick up again, in the doorway, and the old mother is on the kitchen floor. You are in the yard before you have decided anything. {npc} sees you in the moonlight and the stick stops in the air. Severity, the old man said, but measured: the hardest kind there is.

choices.text: Take {him} by the collar in your jaws, carry {him} up the mountain unhurt, and leave {him} on the bare rock all night with you watching

ok.log: A whole night on the rock, with a tiger an arm's length away, breathing. You do not touch {him}. You do not need to. At dawn you carry {him} home and set {him} down at the old mother's feet, and {npc} kneels there and does not get up until noon. The errand is done. The old man of the mountain, far off, nods once.

fail.log: You carry {him} up and leave {him} on the rock, but your hunger walks round {him} all night too, and by dawn you are not sure which of you was being taught. {npc} goes home shaking, and is gentle for a year, and then is not. The errand is not done.

choices.text: Break the arm that holds the stick

effects.log: One bite, clean. {npc} never lifts a stick again; {npc} cannot. The old mother sets the arm with shaking hands, weeping, and says to the empty yard, "It was the arm that carried me to the doctor when I was sick." The errand is done. The old man of the mountain says nothing, which you take to mean it was too much, and enough.

choices.text: Roar once in the doorway, and go

effects.log: The stick drops. The whole village wakes. In the morning {npc} tells everyone a tiger came for the old mother and {npc} drove it off with a stick. The errand is not done.

events.text: Market day in the county town. Through the crowd comes {npc}, with the old mother on {his} back, carrying the old mother the whole ten li to the market to see the jugglers, because the old mother once said, years ago, that it would be nice to see them. The village does not know what to make of it. Neither do you.

choices.text: Follow them home at a distance, on the ridge, all the way

effects.log: Ten li there, ten li back. {npc} does not stop to rest once. At the gate, setting the old mother down, {npc} looks up at your ridge in the dusk, straight at you, and bows. You did not think you could be seen. You can, it seems, by the ones who are looking.

choices.text: Trust nothing. Watch the house another season

effects.log: A season of quiet. The stick is firewood now. You go on watching anyway. Severity that stops watching is only cruelty with a good memory.

events.text: The errand has gone sour while you hesitated. The son who beat the old mother has a child of his own now, and the stick has found the child too. The magpie brings you the case again with its feathers on end, and the old man of the mountain has added something: "Before the frost, or I will find another tiger."

choices.text: Go down tonight, and do it measured, both for the mother and the child

ok.log: A night on the rock, a tiger breathing an arm's length away, and at dawn a man set down at his mother's feet with his own child watching. It is late. It is done. The old man of the mountain nods, not quite as warmly as he would have.

fail.log: You go down and lose your nerve at the fence, or your temper, you are not sure which. The child sees a white tiger and screams. Nothing is done. (-8 health)

choices.text: Refuse the errand. Some houses cannot be mended by a tiger

effects.log: The old man of the mountain looks at you a long time. "Then I will give you a harder one," he says. "That is how errands work." The magpie leaves without a word.

events.text: Snow for three days. The magpie comes with the errand of this stage: a child of the charcoal village went up the mountain for pine needles before the storm and has not come down. The whole village is out with torches on the lower slopes, calling. Higher up, where no torch reaches, another voice is calling the child too: a woman's voice, very sweet, from somewhere ahead in the white. It is not the child's mother. It is a ghost, and it wants a replacement.
events.arc: The Errand: Bring the Lost Home

choices.text: Follow the child's track, what the snow has left of it

ok.log: A scrap of red cloth on a thornbush, a mitten, a hollow under a pine. You find the child before the voice does, curled in a ball with snow on the eyelashes, still breathing.

fail.log: The snow has taken the track. You quarter the slope until your paws bleed, and hear the sweet voice getting closer to something, somewhere above you. (-8 health)

choices.text: Follow the voice instead. It knows where the child is

effects.log: The ghost leads you straight there without meaning to, and turns, and sees you. A woman in white with no feet, a wet face, a voice like honey. Between you, in a hollow under a pine, a child in a red jacket, asleep, which is the dangerous kind of asleep.

choices.text: Roar, so every voice on the mountain stops

effects.log: The ghost stops. So does the child, somewhere: frightened by the roar, it creeps deeper into wherever it is hiding. You have made it quieter, and harder to find.

events.text: The child is in the hollow under the pine, blue at the lips. The ghost in white stands at the edge of the trees and does not come closer while you are there. It can wait. The child cannot. The village torches are an hour below.
events.arc: The Errand: Bring the Lost Home

choices.text: Lie round the child all night, and let the ghost wait

effects.log: You curl round the child in the snow like a white wall, and breathe on it, and the ghost walks round and round you all night singing. At dawn the child wakes warm, looks up into your face, and says, very seriously, "Grandmother?" You carry it down by the jacket to the first torch. The errand is done. (-12 health)

choices.text: Pick the child up by the jacket and run for the torches now

ok.log: Down the mountain in the dark with a child swinging from your jaws like a cub. You leave it in the snow ten paces from the nearest torch and are gone before the shouting starts. The errand is done.

fail.log: The child wakes in your jaws and screams and twists out and runs, back up the slope, toward the sweet voice. You lose it in the trees. (-10 health)

events.text: The ghost in white is still on your mountain, calling. It is not yours: some other tiger's, a long time ago, a woman eaten on the old salt road before you held this ridge, who has been looking for a replacement for two hundred years. Tonight it comes to the edge of your rock and asks, in that sweet voice, why you took the child away from it.
events.arc: The Errand: Bring the Lost Home

choices.text: Find where it fell, and ask the charcoal village to raise a cairn and turn a pot over it

effects.log: Under the snow on the salt road, a few bones. The charcoal village, whose child you carried home, raises the cairn without asking why, turns a rice-steamer over it, and drives the iron spindle through. The sweet voice goes round and round inside, and fainter, and stops. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell it the truth: the child is not for anybody

effects.log: It cries. Ghosts do. It goes away up the mountain and you do not hear it again for a long time, which is not the same as it being gone.

events.text: Another winter, another storm, another child lost on the mountain: a shepherd's child from the far side, out after a strayed goat. The old man of the mountain sends the magpie with the same errand and an edge in it, since the last one went badly. Somewhere in the white a sweet voice has started singing.
events.arc: The Errand: Bring the Lost Home

choices.text: Go into the storm and do not come out without the child

ok.log: You think like a lost child: downhill, out of the wind, toward anything that looks like a door. A cleft in the rock, a child and a goat inside it, both furious. You bring them both down. The errand is done. (-10 health)

fail.log: You find the goat. The village finds the child, alive, at dawn, by itself. The errand is not done, and you are colder than you have been in centuries. (-14 health)

choices.text: Go after the voice and stand between it and the whole mountain

effects.log: You find the ghost and roar it off the mountain for the night. The child comes down on its own at noon. Something was saved. Not the errand. (-8 health)

events.text: The honoured guest has come to the village under your ridge: the smallpox, whom nobody names, whom everybody calls Sonnim, the Guest, or Mama, the Esteemed. In every house with children the families are hosting it with terrible politeness: no quarrels, no washing, no sewing, no loud voices, a bowl of clean water on a little table. They have painted red pocks on the village guardian posts so the Guest will think the village already has it. The mountain god's errand for this stage is to drive it out. The villagers are terrified that you will offend it.

choices.text: Roar it out of the village tonight

ok.log: Your roar goes down the valley like a falling tree. Something in fine clothes leaves the headman's house in a hurry, and two children's fevers break by morning. But the families are horrified: you have shouted at the Guest. Whatever it does next, it will do angry.

fail.log: The Guest does not leave. It does not even look up. It is far older than you. The villagers bar their doors against you instead. (-12 health)

choices.text: Wait for the twelfth night, when they send it off on the straw horse, and walk beside it as escort

effects.log: You lie on the ridge for twelve nights, listening to children cough. On the twelfth the village sets a straw horse at the edge of the road with rice cakes and a little bundle, and the shaman begins the sending-off. You come down.

choices.text: Go into the village in human guise and find where the Guest sits

effects.log: It sits in the best room of the richest house, of course, on a silk cushion, invisible to everyone but you. It looks at your white hair and bows, very correctly. You are expected.

events.text: The Guest stands in the road at the village edge, beside the straw horse, in fine old-fashioned robes with a fan held over its face. Through the gaps in the fan you see the pocks. It bows to you, very correctly. "We are both guests here, Lord of the Mountain," it says. "Both honoured. Both feared. Both take a child sometimes. Shall we not be civil?"

choices.text: "No." Drive it up the road with your teeth

ok.log: A tiger's roar drives evil out; that is the oldest thing anyone knows about tigers. The Guest goes up the road faster than it has ever gone anywhere, fan and all, and the straw horse goes over in the wind of it. No more children sicken. The errand is done.

fail.log: It touches you with the fan. For a month you lie in the den with your white coat coming out in red blotches and every bone on fire. You understand, at last, why the village is polite. (-20 health)

choices.text: Be civil. Escort it out on the straw horse, with honour, to the border of the county

ok.log: You walk beside the straw horse all night, a white tiger escorting a disease to the county border like a magistrate's guest. At the boundary stone it bows again and goes on alone. It does not come back to your valley for a hundred years. The errand is done, and nobody in the village was offended, least of all the Guest.

fail.log: At the boundary stone the Guest turns back, smiling behind the fan, and says it has forgotten something in the village. Civility is a door both ways.

choices.text: Bargain: the children it has not touched yet, for a season of your hunting on the far side

effects.log: It accepts, with a little laugh, and goes, and takes a season of your strength with it. The children it had already touched are not part of the bargain. The errand is not quite done. (-10 health)

events.text: The village under the ridge has come through. Some children are pocked, a few are blind in one eye, two are in the ground, and the rest are running about again shouting, which nobody has dared to do for a month. At the New Year every house hangs a new painting on its gate: a magpie on a pine, and under it a white tiger, enormous, glaring up the road the Guest went.

choices.text: Go and look at the paintings

effects.log: Every one of them is ridiculous, and every one of them has you glaring the right way. You look at them for a long time. Then you go and lie on the ridge above the road the Guest went, glaring, so the paintings are not lying.

choices.text: Visit the two small graves

effects.log: Two mounds the size of rice sacks on the hillside. You lie between them through the first snow. Nobody sees you there, except a magpie, who says nothing for once.

events.text: The Guest has come back to your valley, sooner than anyone expected, in a dry autumn when the children are thin. The pocks are on the guardian posts again, fresh red. The old man of the mountain sends the magpie with one word: "Again."

choices.text: Meet it on the road before it reaches the first house

ok.log: You meet it at the boundary stone at dusk, and this time you do not let it bow first. You walk it back the way it came, civil and enormous, and it goes. The errand is done.

fail.log: It goes round you. It always could. Three children sicken before you find it again. (-15 health)

choices.text: Roar from the ridge every dusk until it goes

effects.log: A month of roaring. The Guest leaves eventually, sulking. So do half the villagers, who cannot sleep. The old man of the mountain says it will do, which means it will not.

events.text: The hunger has eaten the mountain out of you. You are on the rock above the pass at dusk without remembering how you got there. Below, a traveller alone with a lantern and a back frame of dried fish, humming. Nobody else on the road for a mile. Your whole body has already decided. Only you have not.

choices.text: Take the traveller

effects.log: It is over before the lantern hits the ground. In the morning there is a new ghost behind you on the road, humming the same song, and you cannot get it out of your head for a century.

choices.text: Go down to the village pens instead and take an ox

effects.log: An ox is a family's year. You know that, and you take it anyway, and the family will go hungry in your place. It is the least bad thing a hungry tiger can do, and it is not good.

choices.text: Hold yourself on the rock till the lantern is gone, then go north after a bear

effects.log: You dig your claws into the rock until they bleed. The lantern goes down the pass. At dawn you are three ridges north, fighting a bear for its life and yours. You win. Only just. (-15 health)

events.text: Winter, and the hunger has you by the throat. Across the saddle the left ridge is full of deer, fat on the dragon's rain, and the dragon is asleep under the snow. The stream is the line. You agreed that the stream is the line.

choices.text: Cross the stream and hunt the left ridge

effects.log: Three deer before dawn. The dragon does not wake, or pretends not to. In spring there is a stag's skull set very precisely in the middle of the stream, which is a sentence in a language you both speak.

choices.text: Go to the saddle and ask, which you have never done

effects.log: You say it across the stream in the dark: "I am hungry." The dragon opens one eye and says nothing, and in the morning there is a stag on your bank, still warm, with a long tooth-mark in its neck that is not yours.

choices.text: Eat the offering at your own shrine: the pig's head, the rice cakes, all of it

effects.log: The old man of the mountain finds you asleep on the offering rock with rice cake on your whiskers and says, in a tone you have not heard since you were a cub, "Well."

events.text: The villages know you are hungry; they always know. This morning there is a black ox tied to the old pine by your shrine, garlanded with straw rope, and a whole village standing at a respectful distance, not looking at you and not leaving. They have paid you not to come down. You are five hundred years old and they are buying you off with an ox.

choices.text: Accept it, in front of them

effects.log: You take the ox. The village bows and goes home relieved. It is a bargain that works for everyone, and it will be expected, from now on, every bad winter.

choices.text: Accept it, and leave a deer at the headman's gate in the first good month

effects.log: An ox now, a deer in spring, and the village does not know what to make of a god that pays its debts. They start telling a story about it. It is not quite the right story, but it is close.

choices.text: Refuse it. Untie the ox, and go far north to hunt

effects.log: You bite through the straw rope and walk away into the snow. The ox stands there not knowing where to go, which is also what the village does. (-12 health)

events.text: Your ghost comes to you in the hungry dusk, the way changgwi do, very kindly. There is a child on the road below, it says, lost, nobody near. If you take the child, it promises, the ghost goes free; a new one walks behind you; everyone gets what they need. It has your hunger's voice exactly.

choices.text: Let it lead you

effects.log: It leads you. Afterwards the old ghost is not free: ghosts promise, and the pass keeps. The new one is very small, and walks close behind you, and asks you every night when it can go home.

choices.text: Roar it silent, and eat the first thing you can catch that is not human, whatever it is

effects.log: A badger, a crow, half a frozen boar from last autumn. It is enough to get you to morning. The child on the road reaches the next village and never knows. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go down and carry the child home, starving

effects.log: You carry the child by the jacket to the first lit door, with your stomach screaming the whole way, and then you go into the forest and eat snow and bark and a whole nest of field mice. You have never been so hungry or so pleased. (-15 health)

events.text: A hunter has fallen into one of his own pit-traps on your ridge: a stake through the thigh, a broken bow, two dogs barking at the rim. He cannot climb. You are as hungry as you have ever been, and a hunter in a pit is the oldest joke in the mountains.

choices.text: Take him. He dug it for you

effects.log: He dug it for you, and you went in after him, which is a kind of justice and a kind of meal. The ghost that follows you afterwards is furious rather than sad, and keeps trying to warn other hunters, which is almost useful.

choices.text: Pull him out, carry him to the village, and eat his dogs

effects.log: The dogs failed him; that is your verdict on the dogs. The hunter lives, limps, and never digs a pit on your ridge again. In the tavern he tells the story his own way, which makes him the hero and you a great deal larger. (-6 health)

events.text: In human guise you take a cup of barley tea at the county town gate, and the old magistrate {npc} sits down across from you without asking. "White hair, bare feet, eyes like the stream in winter," {npc} says. "My grandmother told me what you look like. I have a case I cannot judge. Two brothers, one sluice gate, a dead ox, and every witness related to both of them. Will you hear it? I will do whatever you say, and sign it with my own name."
events.arc: The Judge Who Could Not Judge

choices.text: Hear it, tonight, by the lamp

ok.log: The elder brother opened the gate; the younger had moved the ditch; the ox drowned because both of them were right, and each was too proud to say so to the other. You order the ditch moved back, the gate shared, and the brothers to buy one ox together. {npc} writes it out and signs it. Legs. It was just.

fail.log: You hear it all night and in the end split it down the middle, which is what {npc} could have done without you, and both of you know it.

choices.text: "A judge who will sign anyone's verdict is not a judge. Hear it yourself, and I will sit with you"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment, then laughs, very tired. "That is what my grandmother said the tiger would say." You sit by the lamp while {npc} judges. It takes all night, and {npc} gets it mostly right.

choices.text: Finish your tea and leave

effects.log: {npc} watches you go down the road and calls after you, "Next autumn, then!" as if you had agreed to something.

events.text: {npc} has another case, and it is the one {npc} has been afraid of for thirty years: the governor's nephew, a burned farmhouse, and a family of five who all say the same thing. If the magistrate judges it rightly, the magistrate will lose the seal, perhaps the head. "I am old," {npc} says. "I want to die a judge. Tell me whether that means doing this."
events.arc: The Judge Who Could Not Judge

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: {npc} judges it rightly. The nephew is sentenced. The governor has the magistrate dismissed by the new moon. On the road out of the county, with one ox cart and the case scrolls, {npc} meets a white tiger sitting at the boundary stone, which walks beside the cart to the next county and leaves without a word.

choices.text: "Judge it, and I will make sure you keep the seal"

effects.log: The governor dreams of a tiger in the yamen yard every night for a month, facing the cell where the nephew sits. The governor does not dismiss anyone. The magistrate dies at seventy-nine, with the seal.

choices.text: "No. Live, and judge the next hundred cases well"

effects.log: {npc} lets the nephew go and judges the next hundred cases very well indeed, and never once looks at you again without looking away.

events.text: A grandchild of the old magistrate {npc} climbs to your shrine with a bundle of case scrolls tied in faded red cord and lays them on the offering rock. "My grandparent's last wish," the grandchild says, "was that these go to the one who sat by the lamp." They are every case the magistrate ever judged, with a small mark beside the ones you heard.
events.arc: The Judge Who Could Not Judge

choices.text: Keep them in the den, and read them in the long winters

effects.npcPass: old age, a judge to the end
effects.log: Forty years of a human court, case by case, in a careful hand. Most of them you would have judged the same way. A few you would have judged worse. You read them every winter until the paper is soft as cloth.

choices.text: Ask the grandchild to sit, and tell you about the magistrate

effects.npcPass: old age, a judge to the end
effects.log: The grandchild talks until dark: a stubborn, frightened, honest old official who kept a bowl of barley tea on the desk for a guest who rarely came. You did not know about the tea. You will think about it for a long time.

events.text: In human guise you walk the autumn market of the county town, and at the medicine stalls you stop. {npc}, an alchemist in dark silk with a lacquered chest, is selling tiger bone: the Hogol elixir, for the joints, for courage, for an old man's vigour. "Real bone," {npc} tells you, "from a striped tiger of the north. But I am looking for better. They say there is a white one in the western mountains. A white tiger's bones would make an elixir for kings." The bones on the tray are real. You know whose they were.

choices.text: Buy the bones, all of them, with a deer left at the stall at dawn

effects.log: In the morning there is a deer at the stall and the tray is empty. You carry the bones of a tiger you once fought for a ridge up into the northern hills and bury them under a pine. {npc} counts the deer twice and decides not to ask.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how one would catch a white tiger, very interested

effects.log: {npc} tells you everything: the poisoned bait, the pit lined with iron, the musket-men, the shaman for the ghosts. You thank {npc} warmly and walk away knowing exactly which roads to watch.

choices.text: Let your eyes go gold for one breath, across the tray

effects.log: {npc} drops the lid of the chest on four fingers and does not even notice. When the shouting is over, the white-haired customer is gone, and the alchemist has a story nobody at the inn believes.

events.text: {npc} has come to your mountain with twelve hired men, an iron-lined pit dug on the deer path, a goat staked over it, and a jar of something that smells like aconite smeared on the goat. {npc} sits by a fire at the foot of the ridge with the lacquered chest open and a pestle ready. "Patience," {npc} tells the hired men. "Tigers get hungry."

choices.text: Free the goat in the night, and fill the pit with the hired men's own boots

effects.log: In the morning the goat is grazing on the ridge, unpoisoned, and the pit is full of twelve pairs of boots. The hired men go home barefoot and quit. {npc} sits by the fire alone and laughs, not entirely happily.

choices.text: Walk into the firelight and sit down across from {npc}

ok.log: You do not speak. You do not need to. {npc} looks at a white tiger sitting across a small fire for an hour, then closes the chest, very slowly, and leaves before dawn. The Hogol elixir in the market is striped tiger bone ever after, and the price goes down.

fail.log: {npc} throws the aconite jar into the fire, and the smoke gets into your eyes and lungs, and you go back up the mountain coughing blood for a week. (-12 health)

choices.text: Take {npc}. A bone-seller among the bones

effects.log: The hired men run. In the morning there is a lacquered chest on its side by the dead fire, and a new ghost on your mountain that walks behind you muttering prices.

events.text: At a roadside teahouse a lean old martial artist in a white training robe sits down at your table, puts an iron staff across it, and studies your face. "I have fought everything in the murim that will fight me," {npc} says. "They tell me the Tiger of Autumn walks these roads as a white-haired stranger, and that when it breathes out, the leaves fall. I would like to see the leaves fall. Once, before I die."

choices.text: "The cliff above the pass, at the equinox. Bring nothing but the staff"

effects.log: {npc} bows over the table, deeply, the bow of a disciple and not of a master. You both know which one of you asked for the lesson.

choices.text: "Go home. You have nothing to prove to a tiger"

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Everything," {npc} says. "I have everything to prove to a tiger, and nothing to anyone else." {npc} pays for your tea and goes, and you suspect this is not over.

events.text: The equinox, the cliff above the pass, red maple leaves knee deep. {npc} is already there, barefoot, the iron staff planted. When you come up out of the pines in your own shape, white and enormous, {npc} smiles like a boy. "Ah," {npc} says. "Good. Now, please, do not hold back."

choices.text: Do not hold back. Breathe out, and let the autumn fall on the cliff

ok.log: You breathe out. Every leaf on the mountain lets go at once, and the staff goes with them, spinning into the gorge. {npc} sits down in the red drift, empty-handed, laughing, crying. "So that is what it looks like," {npc} says. You leave {npc} alive on the cliff, which was always the plan.

fail.log: The iron staff finds the place between your shoulders where the old spear scar is, and for a moment the Tiger of Autumn is on its knees in the leaves. Then you are up, and {npc} lowers the staff, satisfied. "Enough," {npc} says. "Now I have seen it." (-20 health)

choices.text: Fight as an old tiger fights an old master: slowly, and for the pleasure of it

effects.log: All afternoon, staff against paw, neither of you trying to end it. At dusk {npc} stops, out of breath, bows, and says it was the best fight of a long life. You lick a bruised paw and agree.
